chapters.title: Act 1, Scene 1 — Before Leonato’s House
paragraphs: [Enter Leonato, Hero, Beatrice and others, with a Messenger.]
LEONATO. This letter tells me that Don Pedro of Aragon arrives in Messina tonight.
MESSENGER. He's very close by now—he was less than ten miles off when I left him.
LEONATO. How many gentlemen have you lost in this campaign?
MESSENGER. Very few of any rank, and none of note.
LEONATO. A victory is doubled when the winner brings everyone home. I see here that Don Pedro has heaped honor on a young Florentine called Claudio.

MESSENGER. Well deserved on his side, and just as well remembered by Don Pedro. He carried himself far beyond his years—doing the deeds of a lion while looking like a lamb. He's outdone all expectations more than I could possibly tell you.
LEONATO. He has an uncle here in Messina who'll be overjoyed by this.
MESSENGER. I've already delivered him the letters, and he showed great joy—so much joy that it couldn't keep itself modest without breaking into tears.
LEONATO. He burst into tears?
MESSENGER. Plenty of them.
LEONATO. A kind overflow of kindness. No faces are truer than the ones washed that way. How much better to weep at joy than to celebrate weeping!
BEATRICE. Tell me, please—has Signior Stab-and-Thrust come back from the wars or not?
MESSENGER. I don't know anyone by that name, my lady. There was no such person in the whole army.
LEONATO. Who are you asking about, niece?
HERO. My cousin means Signior Benedick of Padua.
MESSENGER. Oh! He's returned, and as cheerful as ever.

BEATRICE. He posted his challenge here in Messina and dared Cupid to an archery match; and my uncle's fool, reading the challenge, signed up for Cupid and challenged him to a duel with blunt arrows. Tell me, how many has he killed and eaten in this war? But—how many has he killed? Because I promised to eat everyone he kills.
LEONATO. Honestly, niece, you're too hard on Signior Benedick; but he'll get even with you, no doubt.
MESSENGER. He's done good service in this war, lady.
BEATRICE. You had stale food, and he helped eat it. He's a brave plate-cleaner—he has an excellent stomach.
MESSENGER. And a good soldier too, my lady.
BEATRICE. A good soldier to a lady, yes. But what's he to a lord?
MESSENGER. A lord to a lord, a man to a man—stuffed with every honorable virtue.
BEATRICE. That's true—he's nothing less than a stuffed man; but as for the stuffing—well, we're all mortal.
LEONATO. Sir, don't misunderstand my niece. There's a kind of merry war between Signior Benedick and her—they never meet without a skirmish of wits.

BEATRICE. Sadly, he gets nothing out of it. In our last clash, four of his five wits went limping off, and now the whole man is governed by just one. So if he has wit enough to keep himself warm, let him show it off as the only thing distinguishing him from his horse—because that's all the wealth he has left to be known as a reasonable creature. Who's his sidekick now? He swears a new brotherhood every month.
MESSENGER. Is that possible?
BEATRICE. Very easily possible. He wears his loyalty like the style of his hat—it changes with whatever's new.
MESSENGER. I see, lady, the gentleman is not in your good books.
BEATRICE. No—and if he were, I'd burn my library. But tell me, who's his companion? Is there no young brawler now who'll travel to the devil with him?
MESSENGER. He's most often in the company of the noble Claudio.

BEATRICE. Oh Lord—he'll cling to him like a disease. He's caught faster than the plague, and whoever catches him goes mad on the spot. God help noble Claudio! If he's caught the Benedick, it'll cost him a thousand pounds before he's cured.
MESSENGER. I'll stay on your good side, lady.
BEATRICE. Do that, my friend.
LEONATO. You'll never go mad, niece.
BEATRICE. No—not until January gets hot.
MESSENGER. Don Pedro is approaching.
[Enter Don Pedro, Don John, Claudio, Benedick, Balthasar and others.]
DON PEDRO. Good Signior Leonato, you've come out to meet your own trouble. The fashion of the world is to avoid expense, and here you go embracing it.
LEONATO. Trouble never came to my house in the shape of your Grace; for once trouble's gone, comfort should remain. But when you leave me, sorrow stays behind and happiness takes its leave.
DON PEDRO. You take on your burden too willingly. I think this is your daughter.
LEONATO. Her mother has told me so many times.
BENEDICK. Were you in doubt, sir, that you had to ask her?
LEONATO. No, Signior Benedick—because then you were just a child.
DON PEDRO. There you have it, Benedick. We can guess from this what kind of man you are. The lady takes after her father, plainly. Be glad of it, lady—you look like an honorable father.
BENEDICK. If Signior Leonato is her father, she still wouldn't wear his head on her shoulders for all of Messina—much as she looks like him.
BEATRICE. I'm amazed you keep talking, Signior Benedick—nobody's listening to you.
BENEDICK. What! My dear Lady Disdain, are you still alive?
BEATRICE. How could Disdain ever die while she has such suitable food as Signior Benedick to feed her? Courtesy itself must turn into disdain the moment you arrive.
BENEDICK. Then courtesy is a traitor. But it's a fact: I'm loved by every lady—you alone excepted. And I wish I could find it in my heart not to have a hard heart, because truly, I love none of them.

BEATRICE. A great relief to women—otherwise they'd be pestered by a dangerous suitor. I thank God and my cold blood, I share your feeling there. I'd rather hear my dog bark at a crow than listen to a man swear he loves me.
BENEDICK. May God keep your Ladyship in that frame of mind—so some gentleman somewhere will be spared a predestined scratched face.
BEATRICE. Scratching couldn't make it worse, if the face were anything like yours.
BENEDICK. Well, you're a rare teacher of parrots.
BEATRICE. A bird of my tongue is better than a beast of yours.
BENEDICK. I wish my horse had the speed of your tongue, and the same staying power. But keep going, in God's name—I'm done.
BEATRICE. You always end with a worn-out trick. I know you of old.

DON PEDRO. That's the gist of it, Leonato. Signior Claudio and Signior Benedick—my dear friend Leonato has invited you all. I tell him we'll stay here at least a month, and he heartily prays some occasion will keep us longer. I'll swear he's no hypocrite—he prays from the heart.
LEONATO. If you swear it, my lord, you won't be forsworn. [To Don John] Let me welcome you, my lord: now that you're reconciled with the Prince your brother, I owe you every duty.
DON JOHN. I thank you. I'm not a man of many words, but I thank you.
LEONATO. Will your Grace lead the way?
DON PEDRO. Give me your hand, Leonato. We'll go together.
[Exit all but Benedick and Claudio.]
CLAUDIO. Benedick, did you notice Signior Leonato's daughter?
BENEDICK. I didn't take notice of her, but I looked at her.
CLAUDIO. Isn't she a modest young lady?
BENEDICK. Are you asking me as an honest man for my honest opinion, or do you want me to speak the usual way—as the self-declared tyrant of their sex?
CLAUDIO. No—please, speak in plain judgment.

BENEDICK. Well, honestly, I think she's too short for high praise, too dark for fair praise, and too small for great praise. The only compliment I can pay her is that if she were anything but what she is, she'd be ugly; and being only what she is, I don't like her.
CLAUDIO. You think I'm joking. Please—tell me truly how you like her.
BENEDICK. Are you looking to buy her, that you ask after her so closely?
CLAUDIO. Could the world buy such a jewel?

BENEDICK. Sure—and a case to keep it in. But are you saying this with a serious face, or are you playing the mocker—telling us Cupid's a good rabbit-catcher and Vulcan's a fine carpenter? Come on, what tune do I sing along to?
CLAUDIO. To my eye, she's the sweetest lady I've ever seen.

BENEDICK. I can still see without glasses, and I see no such thing. There's her cousin—if she weren't possessed by a fury—who outshines her in beauty as much as the first of May outshines the last of December. But I hope you don't actually intend to become a husband?
CLAUDIO. I'd hardly trust myself, even if I'd sworn the opposite, if Hero would be my wife.

BENEDICK. Has it come to this? Hasn't the world got one man who won't put on the cap of suspicion? Will I never see a bachelor of sixty again? Go on, then—if you absolutely must shove your neck into the yoke, wear the mark of it and sigh away your Sundays.
[Re-enter Don Pedro.]
Look! Don Pedro's come back to find you.
DON PEDRO. What secret has kept you here, that you didn't follow to Leonato's?
BENEDICK. I wish your Grace would force me to tell.
DON PEDRO. I charge you, on your allegiance.

BENEDICK. You hear that, Count Claudio? I can be as secret as a mute man—I want you to believe so. But on my allegiance, mark this, on my allegiance: he is in love. With whom? Now that's your Grace's part to ask. Notice how short his answer is: with Hero, Leonato's short daughter.
CLAUDIO. If that were true, that would be how it was put.
BENEDICK. Like the old tale, my lord: 'It is not so, nor was it so; but indeed, God forbid it should be so.'
CLAUDIO. If my feelings don't change soon, God forbid it should be otherwise.
DON PEDRO. Amen, if you love her—the lady is very much worthy.
CLAUDIO. You say this to lure me in, my lord.
DON PEDRO. By my honor, I speak my mind.
CLAUDIO. And honestly, my lord, I spoke mine.
BENEDICK. And by my two honors and oaths, my lord, I spoke mine.
CLAUDIO. That I love her, I feel.
DON PEDRO. That she is worthy, I know.
BENEDICK. That I neither feel how she could be loved nor know how she could be worthy—that opinion no fire can melt out of me. I'd die holding it at the stake.
DON PEDRO. You were always a stubborn heretic when it came to beauty.
CLAUDIO. And he could only maintain his position by sheer willpower.

BENEDICK. That a woman conceived me, I thank her. That she brought me up, I likewise give her my most humble thanks. But that I would let a hunter's horn be blown on my forehead, or wear a bugle on an invisible strap—all women must pardon me. Because I won't do them the wrong of mistrusting any of them, I'll do myself the right of trusting none. And the upshot—for which I may go better dressed—is: I'll live a bachelor.
DON PEDRO. I'll see you turn pale with love before I die.

BENEDICK. With anger, with sickness, or with hunger, my lord—not with love. If I ever lose more blood to love than I can replace with drink, then poke out my eyes with a ballad-writer's pen and hang me at the door of a brothel as the sign of blind Cupid.
DON PEDRO. Well, if you ever fall from this conviction, you'll make a famous case study.
BENEDICK. If I do, hang me in a bottle like a cat and shoot at me; and whoever hits me, let him be clapped on the shoulder and called Adam.
DON PEDRO. Well, time will tell: 'In time the wild bull bears the yoke.'

BENEDICK. The wild bull may; but if the sensible Benedick ever does, pluck the bull's horns off and put them on my forehead. Let me be painted hideously, and in big letters like the ones that say 'Here's a good horse for hire,' let them write under my sign: 'Here you may see Benedick the married man.'
CLAUDIO. If that ever happened, you'd go horn-mad.
DON PEDRO. Well, if Cupid hasn't emptied his quiver in Venice, you'll be trembling for this soon.
BENEDICK. Then I expect an earthquake too.

DON PEDRO. Well—you'll come around in time. In the meantime, good Signior Benedick, get yourself to Leonato's. Send him my regards, and tell him I won't fail him at supper. He's made great preparations.
BENEDICK. I've got just about enough wit in me for that errand. And so I commit you—
CLAUDIO. To the care of God: from my house, if I had one—
DON PEDRO. The sixth of July: your loving friend, Benedick.

BENEDICK. No, no, don't mock. The substance of your talk is sometimes patched with scraps, and the patches are only loosely sewn on either. Before you mock old tags any further, examine your conscience. And so I leave you.
[Exit.]
CLAUDIO. My liege, your Highness can do me a favor now.
DON PEDRO. My love is yours to instruct: just teach it how, and you'll see how readily it learns any hard lesson that does you good.
CLAUDIO. Does Leonato have a son, my lord?
DON PEDRO. No child but Hero—she's his only heir. Are you in love with her, Claudio?

CLAUDIO. Oh, my lord, when you set out on this campaign that's now ended, I looked at her with a soldier's eye that liked what it saw, but had rougher work in hand than pushing fondness into love. Now I'm back, and the war thoughts have vacated their places—and into their rooms come crowding soft and delicate desires, all reminding me how lovely young Hero is, telling me I liked her before I went to war.

DON PEDRO. You'll act the lover any minute now and tire the listener with a whole book of words. If you love fair Hero, hold on to it—I'll speak with her, and with her father, and you shall have her. Wasn't that the point of weaving such a fine story?
CLAUDIO. How sweetly you minister to love—you who know love's grief by its very look! But just so my feelings don't seem too sudden, I'd have softened them with a longer speech.

DON PEDRO. Why make the bridge much wider than the river? The best gift is what's needed. Look—what serves the purpose is what fits. The point is, you love her, and I'll provide you the remedy. I know there'll be revelry tonight. I'll take your part in some disguise and tell fair Hero I am Claudio. To her face I'll open my heart and take her hearing captive with the force of my amorous tale. Then I'll go to her father afterward—and the conclusion is, she shall be yours. Let's put it into practice right away.
[Exit.]

chapters.title: Act 1, Scene 2 — A room in Leonato’s house
paragraphs: [Enter Leonato and Antonio, meeting.]
LEONATO. Well, brother? Where's my nephew, your son? Has he arranged the music?
ANTONIO. He's very busy with it. But, brother, I can tell you strange news you haven't even dreamed of.
LEONATO. Is it good news?

ANTONIO. As the outcome will determine—but it has a fine cover, and looks well from the outside. The Prince and Count Claudio, walking down a thickly-hedged path in my orchard, were overheard by one of my men, who caught this much: the Prince told Claudio that he loved my niece, your daughter, and meant to announce it tonight at a dance; and if he found her agreeable, he meant to seize the moment at once and bring it up with you.
LEONATO. Did the fellow who told you this have any sense?
ANTONIO. A good sharp fellow. I'll send for him, and you can question him yourself.

LEONATO. No, no—we'll treat it as a dream until it shows itself. But I'll tell my daughter about it, so she can be better prepared with an answer, in case this turns out to be true. Go and tell her of it.
[Several persons cross the stage.]
Cousins, you know what you have to do. Oh, I beg your pardon, friend; come with me, and I'll make use of your skill. Good cousin, take care during this busy time.
[Exit.]

chapters.title: Act 1, Scene 3 — Another room in Leonato’s house
paragraphs: [Enter Don John and Conrade.]
CONRADE. What in the world, my lord! Why are you so excessively sad?
DON JOHN. There's no measure in the cause that produces it, so the sadness has no limit either.
CONRADE. You should listen to reason.
DON JOHN. And once I've listened to it, what blessings does it bring?
CONRADE. If not an immediate cure, at least patient endurance.

DON JOHN. I'm amazed that you—since, as you say, you were born under Saturn—are trying to apply a moral medicine to a deadly affliction. I can't hide what I am: I must be sad when I have cause, and not smile at anyone's jokes; eat when I'm hungry, and not wait on anyone's schedule; sleep when I'm drowsy, and not mind anyone's business; laugh when I'm cheerful, and not flatter anyone's mood.

CONRADE. Yes; but you mustn't show it openly until you can do so without consequences. You've recently stood opposed to your brother, and he has just taken you back into his favor; you can't take real root there except in fair weather you create yourself. You need to shape the season for your own harvest.

DON JOHN. I'd rather be a worm in a hedge than a rose in his good graces; and it suits my temperament better to be disdained by everyone than to fashion myself a manner that steals love from anyone. In this, although I can't be called a flattering honest man, it can't be denied that I'm a plain-dealing villain. I'm trusted with a muzzle and freed with a clog on my leg—so I've decided not to sing in my cage. If I had my mouth free, I'd bite; if I had my liberty, I'd do as I pleased. In the meantime, let me be what I am, and don't try to change me.
CONRADE. Can't you make any use of your discontent?
DON JOHN. I make every use of it—it's all I use. Who's coming here?
[Enter Borachio.]
What's the news, Borachio?
BORACHIO. I just came from a great supper. The Prince, your brother, is being royally entertained by Leonato, and I can give you news of an intended marriage.
DON JOHN. Will it serve as a foundation to build mischief on? What kind of fool engages himself to a life of trouble?
BORACHIO. Why, it's your brother's right-hand man.
DON JOHN. Who? The most exquisite Claudio?
BORACHIO. The very same.
DON JOHN. A proper young gentleman! And whom—whom does he have his eye on?
BORACHIO. Why, Hero—the daughter and heir of Leonato.
DON JOHN. A very forward little March-chick! How did you come to know this?

BORACHIO. While I was hired as a perfumer and was fumigating a musty room, in came the Prince and Claudio, hand in hand, deep in serious conference. I slipped behind the wall-hanging and there I heard them agree that the Prince would woo Hero for himself, and once he'd won her, hand her over to Count Claudio.

DON JOHN. Come, come—let's go there. This may turn out to be food for my resentment. That young upstart has all the glory from my overthrow; if I can thwart him any way, I bless myself in every way. Are you both reliable, and will you help me?
CONRADE. To the death, my lord.
DON JOHN. Let's go to the great supper. Their cheer is all the greater because I've been put down. I wish the cook were on my side! Shall we go and see what can be done?
BORACHIO. We're at your Lordship's service.
[Exit.]

chapters.title: Act 2, Scene 1 — A hall in Leonato’s house
paragraphs: [Enter Leonato, Antonio, Hero, Beatrice and others.]
LEONATO. Wasn't Count John here at supper?
ANTONIO. I didn't see him.
BEATRICE. How sour that gentleman looks! I never see him without getting heartburn for an hour afterwards.
HERO. He has a very melancholy disposition.

BEATRICE. He'd be an excellent man if he were made exactly halfway between him and Benedick: the one is too much like a statue and says nothing; the other is too much like my lady's eldest son, always chattering.
LEONATO. So half of Signior Benedick's tongue in Count John's mouth, and half of Count John's melancholy in Signior Benedick's face—
BEATRICE. With a good leg and a good foot, uncle, and enough money in his purse—such a man could win any woman in the world, if he could win her goodwill.
LEONATO. Honestly, niece, you'll never get a husband if you're so sharp-tongued.
ANTONIO. In truth, she's too sharp.
BEATRICE. Too sharp is worse than just sharp—I'll reduce God's gift on that side; for the saying is, 'God sends a sharp cow short horns'; but to a cow that's too sharp, He sends none at all.
LEONATO. So by being too sharp, God will send you no horns?
BEATRICE. Exactly—if He sends me no husband; for which blessing I'm on my knees to Him every morning and evening. Lord! I couldn't stand a husband with a beard on his face. I'd rather sleep in wool.
LEONATO. You may find a husband with no beard.

BEATRICE. What would I do with him? Dress him in my clothes and make him my lady-in-waiting? A man with a beard is more than a youth, and a man without a beard is less than a man. He that is more than a youth isn't for me; and he that is less than a man, I am not for him. So I'll just take sixpence as a down payment from the bear-keeper, and lead his apes into hell.
LEONATO. Well then, are you going into hell?

BEATRICE. No—just to the gate. And there the Devil will meet me, like an old cuckold, with horns on his head, and say, 'Off you go to heaven, Beatrice, off to heaven; there's no room here for you maids.' So I hand over my apes, and away to Saint Peter for heaven. He shows me where the bachelors sit, and we live there as merry as the day is long.
ANTONIO.
[To Hero.] Well, niece, I trust you'll be guided by your father.

BEATRICE. Yes, indeed; it's my cousin's duty to curtsy and say, 'Father, as it please you.' But for all that, cousin, let him be a handsome fellow, or else make another curtsy and say, 'Father, as it pleases me.'
LEONATO. Well, niece, I hope to see you one day fitted out with a husband.

BEATRICE. Not until God makes men of some other material than earth. Wouldn't it grieve a woman to be mastered by a piece of valiant dust? To give account of her life to a clod of wayward clay? No, uncle, I'll have none of it. Adam's sons are my brothers—and honestly, I consider it a sin to marry one of my kin.
LEONATO. Daughter, remember what I told you: if the Prince should approach you that way, you know what to answer.

BEATRICE. The fault will lie with the music, cousin, if you aren't wooed in good time. If the Prince is too pressing, tell him there's measure in everything, and dance out your answer. Because listen, Hero: wooing, wedding, and repenting are like a Scotch jig, a measure, and a cinquepace. The first courtship is hot and hasty like a Scotch jig, and just as fantastical; the wedding mannerly and modest like a measure, full of state and old ceremony; and then comes Repentance, who, with his bad legs, falls into the cinquepace faster and faster until he sinks into his grave.
LEONATO. Cousin, you grasp things very shrewdly.
BEATRICE. I have good eyes, uncle—I can see a church by daylight.
LEONATO. The revellers are coming in, brother. Make room.
[Enter Don Pedro, Claudio, Benedick, Balthasar, Don John, Borachio, Margaret, Ursula and others, masked.]
DON PEDRO. Lady, will you take a turn with your friend?
HERO. As long as you walk softly, look kindly, and say nothing, I'm yours for the walk—especially when I walk away.
DON PEDRO. With me as your company?
HERO. I may say so when I choose.
DON PEDRO. And when will it please you to say so?
HERO. When I like your face; for God forbid the lute should be like the case!
DON PEDRO. My mask is Philemon's roof; inside the house is Jove.
HERO. Why then, your mask should be thatched.
DON PEDRO. Speak low, if you speak of love.
[Takes her aside.]
BALTHASAR. Well, I wish you liked me.
MARGARET. I wouldn't, for your own sake—I have many bad qualities.
BALTHASAR. Such as?
MARGARET. I say my prayers out loud.
BALTHASAR. I like you all the better—the listeners can say Amen.
MARGARET. God give me a good dancer to match with!
BALTHASAR. Amen.
MARGARET. And God keep him out of my sight when the dance is done! Answer, clerk.
BALTHASAR. No more words: the clerk has answered.
URSULA. I know you well enough—you're Signior Antonio.
ANTONIO. In a word, I'm not.
URSULA. I know you by the wagging of your head.
ANTONIO. To tell you the truth, I'm imitating him.
URSULA. You could never imitate him so badly-well, unless you were the very man. Here's his dry hand, up and down—it's you, it's you.
ANTONIO. In a word, I'm not.
URSULA. Come, come; do you think I don't know you by your excellent wit? Can virtue hide itself? Go on—hush, it's you. Graces will show, and there's an end of it.
BEATRICE. Will you not tell me who told you so?
BENEDICK. No, you'll have to excuse me.
BEATRICE. And you won't tell me who you are?
BENEDICK. Not now.
BEATRICE. That I was disdainful, and that I got my good wit out of the 'Hundred Merry Tales.' Well, this was Signior Benedick that said so.
BENEDICK. Who's he?
BEATRICE. I'm sure you know him well enough.
BENEDICK. Not I, believe me.
BEATRICE. Has he never made you laugh?
BENEDICK. Please—who is he?

BEATRICE. Why, he's the Prince's jester—a very dull fool. His only gift is in inventing impossible slanders; only libertines enjoy him, and what they admire isn't his wit but his villainy. He pleases men and then angers them, and then they laugh at him and beat him. I'm sure he's in this fleet—I wish he'd boarded me!
BENEDICK. When I know the gentleman, I'll tell him what you say.

BEATRICE. Do, do. He'll just crack a comparison or two against me—which, if not noticed or not laughed at, throws him into melancholy. And then there's a partridge wing saved, because the fool will eat no supper that night. [Music within.] We must follow the leaders.
BENEDICK. In every good thing.
BEATRICE. No—if they lead to any ill, I'll leave them at the next turn.
[Dance. Then exit all but Don John, Borachio and Claudio.]
DON JOHN. Surely my brother is in love with Hero, and has taken her father aside to discuss it with him. The ladies follow her, and only one masked man remains.
BORACHIO. And that's Claudio—I know him by his bearing.
DON JOHN. Aren't you Signior Benedick?
CLAUDIO. You know me well; I am he.

DON JOHN. Signior, you're very close to my brother in his love. He's in love with Hero. I beg you, dissuade him from her—she's no equal match for his birth. You'd be doing the part of an honest man in it.
CLAUDIO. How do you know he loves her?
DON JOHN. I heard him swear his affection.
BORACHIO. So did I; and he swore he'd marry her tonight.
DON JOHN. Come, let's to the banquet.
[Exit Don John and Borachio.]

CLAUDIO. I answer this in the name of Benedick, but I hear this bad news with the ears of Claudio. So it's certain—the Prince is wooing for himself. Friendship is constant in all other matters, except in the business and affairs of love. Therefore all hearts in love use their own tongues. Let every eye negotiate for itself and trust no agent—for beauty is a witch against whose charms loyalty melts into blood. This is a hazard proved every hour, which I didn't suspect. So farewell, Hero!
[Re-enter Benedick.]
BENEDICK. Count Claudio?
CLAUDIO. Yes, the same.
BENEDICK. Come, will you go with me?
CLAUDIO. Where?

BENEDICK. Just to the nearest willow, about your own business, Count. How will you wear the garland? Around your neck, like a usurer's chain? Or under your arm, like a lieutenant's scarf? You'll have to wear it one way or another, because the Prince has got your Hero.
CLAUDIO. I wish him joy of her.
BENEDICK. Why, that's spoken like an honest cattle-dealer—that's how they sell bullocks. But did you think the Prince would have served you this way?
CLAUDIO. Please, leave me alone.
BENEDICK. Ha! Now you're striking like the blind man—it was the boy who stole your food, and you'll beat the post.
CLAUDIO. If you won't go, I'll leave you.
[Exit.]

BENEDICK. Alas! Poor wounded bird. Now he'll creep into the rushes. But that my Lady Beatrice should know me and not know me! The Prince's fool! Ha! Maybe I go under that title because I'm merry. Yes, but if I do, I'm wronging myself; that's not my reputation. It's the base though bitter disposition of Beatrice that projects the world into her person, and so makes me out that way. Well, I'll get my revenge as best I can.
[Re-enter Don Pedro.]
DON PEDRO. Now, signior, where's the Count? Did you see him?

BENEDICK. Honestly, my lord, I've played the part of Lady Rumor. I found him here as melancholy as a hunting lodge in a deserted park. I told him—and I think I told him truly—that your Grace had won the goodwill of this young lady, and I offered him my company to a willow tree, either to make him a garland, as one forsaken, or to bind him up a switch, as deserving to be whipped.
DON PEDRO. To be whipped! What's his fault?
BENEDICK. The simple offense of a schoolboy who, overjoyed at finding a bird's nest, shows it to his companion—and the companion steals it.
DON PEDRO. Would you make a trust into a transgression? The transgression is in the thief.

BENEDICK. Still, it wouldn't have been amiss to make both the switch and the garland. The garland he might have worn himself, and the switch he might have bestowed on you—who, as I see it, have stolen his bird's nest.
DON PEDRO. I'm only going to teach them to sing, and return them to the owner.
BENEDICK. If their singing matches your saying, then by my honor, you speak truly.
DON PEDRO. The Lady Beatrice has a quarrel with you—the gentleman who danced with her told her you've greatly wronged her.

BENEDICK. Oh! She insulted me beyond what a block of wood could endure. An oak with only one green leaf on it would have answered her back. My very mask began to come alive and scold her. She told me, not realizing it was me, that I was the Prince's jester, that I was duller than a great thaw—piling joke on joke against me with such an impossible delivery that I stood there like a man at target practice with a whole army shooting at me. She speaks daggers, and every word stabs. If her breath were as terrible as her conclusions, no one could live near her—she'd infect everything up to the North Star. I wouldn't marry her, even if she were endowed with everything Adam had before he sinned. She'd have set Hercules to turning the spit—yes, and split his club to make the fire too. Come, don't speak of her. You'll find her to be the infernal Ate in fine clothes. I wish to God some scholar would conjure her away, because as long as she's here, a man can live as peacefully in hell as in a sanctuary; and people sin on purpose just to go there. So indeed, all unrest, horror and disturbance follow her.
[Re-enter Claudio, Beatrice, Hero and Leonato.]
DON PEDRO. Look! Here she comes.

BENEDICK. Will your Grace command me any errand to the world's end? I'll go on the slightest errand right now to the Antipodes that you can devise; I'll fetch you a toothpick from the furthest corner of Asia, bring you the measurement of Prester John's foot, fetch you a hair from the Great Khan's beard, do you any embassy to the Pygmies, rather than hold three words' conversation with this harpy. Do you have any work for me?
DON PEDRO. None, except to desire your good company.
BENEDICK. Oh God, sir, here's a dish I don't enjoy—I can't stand my Lady Tongue.
[Exit.]
DON PEDRO. Come, lady, come; you've lost the heart of Signior Benedick.

BEATRICE. Indeed, my lord, he lent it to me for a while; and I gave him interest on it—a double heart for his single one. But once before, he won it off me with loaded dice, so your Grace may well say I've lost it.
DON PEDRO. You've put him down, lady, you've put him down.
BEATRICE. I wouldn't want him to do that to me, my lord, in case I should turn out the mother of fools. I've brought Count Claudio, whom you sent me to find.
DON PEDRO. Why, what now, Count! Why are you sad?
CLAUDIO. Not sad, my lord.
DON PEDRO. What then? Sick?
CLAUDIO. Neither, my lord.
BEATRICE. The Count is neither sad, nor sick, nor merry, nor well. But Seville Count, sour as a Seville orange, and something of that jealous complexion.

DON PEDRO. Honestly, lady, I think your description is true; though I'd swear, if he is so, his suspicion is false. Here, Claudio—I've wooed in your name, and fair Hero is won. I've spoken with her father, and his goodwill is obtained. Name the day of the wedding, and may God give you joy!
LEONATO. Count, take my daughter from me, and with her my fortunes. His Grace has made the match, and may all grace say Amen to it!
BEATRICE. Speak, Count, it's your cue.
CLAUDIO. Silence is the most perfect herald of joy. I'd be little happy if I could tell how much. Lady, just as you are mine, I am yours. I give myself away for you and dote on the exchange.
BEATRICE. Speak, cousin—or if you can't, stop his mouth with a kiss and let him not speak either.
DON PEDRO. Indeed, lady, you have a merry heart.
BEATRICE. Yes, my lord—I thank it, poor fool, it keeps on the windward side of care. My cousin tells him in his ear that he is in her heart.
CLAUDIO. And so she does, cousin.
BEATRICE. Good Lord, everyone matched up! So everyone goes off to the world but me, and I'm sunburnt and unwanted. I may sit in a corner and cry heigh-ho for a husband!
DON PEDRO. Lady Beatrice, I'll get you one.
BEATRICE. I'd rather have one of your father's getting. Has your Grace got a brother like you? Your father produced excellent husbands, if a maid could get hold of them.
DON PEDRO. Will you have me, lady?

BEATRICE. No, my lord, unless I could have another for working days. Your Grace is too expensive to wear every day. But I beg your Grace, pardon me—I was born to speak nothing but mirth and no real substance.
DON PEDRO. Your silence offends me most, and being merry suits you best—without question, you were born in a merry hour.
BEATRICE. No, truly, my lord, my mother cried; but then there was a star dancing, and under that I was born. Cousins, God give you joy!
LEONATO. Niece, will you see to those things I told you about?
BEATRICE. I beg your pardon, uncle. By your Grace's leave.
[Exit.]
DON PEDRO. Honestly, a pleasantly spirited lady.

LEONATO. There's little of the melancholy element in her, my lord. She's never sad except when she sleeps, and not even sad then—I've heard my daughter say she has often dreamed of unhappiness and woken herself up with laughing.
DON PEDRO. She can't bear to hear talk of a husband.
LEONATO. Oh! By no means—she mocks all her suitors out of pursuing her.
DON PEDRO. She'd make an excellent wife for Benedick.
LEONATO. Oh Lord, my lord! If they were married a week, they'd talk themselves mad.
DON PEDRO. Count Claudio, when do you mean to go to church?
CLAUDIO. Tomorrow, my lord. Time goes on crutches until love has all its rites.
LEONATO. Not till Monday, my dear son, which is exactly a week from now—and a time too brief, even so, to have everything in order to my liking.

DON PEDRO. Come, you shake your head at so long a wait. But I promise you, Claudio, the time won't go dully by us. In the interim, I'll undertake one of Hercules' labors—which is to bring Signior Benedick and the Lady Beatrice into a mountain of affection for each other. I'd very much like a match between them, and I don't doubt I can shape it, if you three will just give me the assistance I direct.
LEONATO. My lord, I'm with you, though it cost me ten nights of sleeplessness.
CLAUDIO. And I, my lord.
DON PEDRO. And you too, gentle Hero?
HERO. I'll do any modest office, my lord, to help my cousin to a good husband.

DON PEDRO. And Benedick is not the most hopeless husband I know. I can praise him this far: he's of a noble strain, of proven valor, and confirmed honesty. I'll teach you how to play upon your cousin so that she'll fall in love with Benedick; and I, with your two helps, will so work on Benedick that, despite his quick wit and his queasy stomach, he'll fall in love with Beatrice. If we can do this, Cupid is no longer an archer—his glory shall be ours, because we'll be the only love-gods. Come in with me, and I'll tell you my plan.
[Exit.]

chapters.title: Act 2, Scene 2 — Another room in Leonato’s house
paragraphs: [Enter Don John and Borachio.]
DON JOHN. So it is—Count Claudio is to marry Leonato's daughter.
BORACHIO. Yes, my lord; but I can spoil it.

DON JOHN. Any obstacle, any crosscurrent, any impediment will be medicine to me. I'm sick with displeasure toward him, and whatever cuts across his happiness lines up exactly with mine. How can you wreck this marriage?
BORACHIO. Not honestly, my lord—but so covertly that no dishonesty will show on me.
DON JOHN. Tell me briefly how.
BORACHIO. I think I told your lordship, a year ago, how much I'm in the good graces of Margaret, Hero's waiting-gentlewoman.
DON JOHN. I remember.
BORACHIO. I can, at any unseasonable hour of the night, arrange for her to look out at her lady's chamber window.
DON JOHN. What life is in that, that can mean the death of this marriage?

BORACHIO. The poison in it is yours to mix. Go to the Prince your brother; don't hold back from telling him that he has wronged his own honor by marrying off the renowned Claudio—whose reputation you greatly uphold—to a contaminated whore, the likes of Hero.
DON JOHN. What proof can I give of that?
BORACHIO. Proof enough to outrage the Prince, to torment Claudio, to ruin Hero, and to kill Leonato. Do you look for any other outcome?
DON JOHN. Just to spite them, I'd attempt anything.

BORACHIO. Go then. Find me a suitable hour to draw Don Pedro and Count Claudio aside; tell them that you know Hero loves me. Show a kind of zeal toward both the Prince and Claudio, as if—out of love for your brother's honor, who has made this match, and your friend's reputation, who is thus about to be deceived by the false appearance of a maid—you've discovered this fact. They'll hardly believe it without proof. Offer them evidence as concrete as this: seeing me at her chamber window, hearing me call Margaret 'Hero,' and hearing Margaret call me 'Claudio.' Bring them to see this on the very night before the planned wedding. In the meantime, I'll so arrange things that Hero will be absent, and there'll appear such seeming proof of Hero's disloyalty that jealousy will be called certainty, and the whole preparation overthrown.
DON JOHN. Whatever bad outcome may grow from this, I'll put it into practice. Be cunning in carrying it out, and your fee is a thousand ducats.
BORACHIO. You stay firm in the accusation, and my cunning won't shame me.
DON JOHN. I'll go right now and learn the day of their marriage.
[Exit.]

chapters.title: Act 2, Scene 3 — Leonato’s Garden
paragraphs: [Enter Benedick.]
BENEDICK. Boy!
[Enter a Boy.]
BOY. Signior?
BENEDICK. There's a book in my chamber window—bring it to me here in the orchard.
BOY. I'm here already, sir.
BENEDICK. I know that; but I want you gone, and back again.
[Exit Boy.]

It really amazes me that one man, seeing how much another man becomes a fool when he dedicates his behavior to love, will—after he's laughed at such shallow follies in others—make himself the subject of his own scorn by falling in love. And such a man is Claudio. I have known him when he cared for no music except the drum and the fife; and now he'd rather hear the tabor and the pipe. I have known him to walk ten miles on foot to see a good suit of armor; and now he'll lie awake ten nights designing the cut of a new doublet. He used to speak plainly and to the point, like an honest man and a soldier; and now he's turned into mere wordplay. His words are a fantastical banquet—nothing but strange dishes. Can I be so converted, and see with these eyes? I can't say; I think not. I won't swear that love won't transform me into an oyster, but I'll take my oath: until he has made an oyster of me, he'll never make me such a fool. One woman is beautiful—yet I'm fine; another is wise—yet I'm fine; another virtuous—yet I'm fine. But until all those graces are in one woman, no woman shall come into my graces. Rich she must be, that's certain; wise, or I'll have none of her; virtuous, or I'll never make a bid for her; beautiful, or I'll never look at her; mild, or don't come near me; noble, or I'm not interested even for an angel; of good conversation, an excellent musician—and her hair can be whatever color it pleases God. Ha! The Prince and Monsieur Love! I'll hide in the arbor.
[Withdraws.]
[Enter Don Pedro, Leonato and Claudio, followed by Balthasar and Musicians.]
DON PEDRO. Come, shall we hear this music?
CLAUDIO. Yes, my good lord. How still the evening is—as if hushed on purpose to grace the harmony!
DON PEDRO. Do you see where Benedick has hidden himself?
CLAUDIO. Oh! Very well, my lord. Once the music ends, we'll give the young fox his money's worth.
DON PEDRO. Come, Balthasar, we'll hear that song again.
BALTHASAR. Oh, good my lord, don't tax so poor a voice to slander music more than once.
DON PEDRO. It's always the sign of excellence to put on a strange face about one's own perfection. Please—sing, and let me woo no more.
BALTHASAR. Because you talk of wooing, I'll sing—since many a wooer begins his suit with someone he doesn't think worthy; yet he woos; yet he'll swear he loves.
DON PEDRO. No, please, come on. Or if you want to argue longer, do it in notes.
BALTHASAR. Note this before my notes: there's not a note of mine that's worth the noting.
DON PEDRO. Why, these are very crotchets he speaks—notes, notes, indeed, and nothing!
[Music.]
BENEDICK. Now, divine air! Now his soul is ravished! Isn't it strange that sheep's guts should haul souls out of men's bodies? Well, give me a horn for my money, when all's done.

BALTHASAR [sings.] Sigh no more, ladies, sigh no more, men were always deceivers; one foot in sea, and one on shore, to one thing never constant. Then sigh no more, but let them go, and be cheerful and bonny, converting all your sounds of grief into Hey nonny, nonny.

Sing no more songs, sing no more of glooms so dull and heavy; the fraud of men was ever so, since summer first turned leafy. Then sigh no more, but let them go, and be cheerful and bonny, converting all your sounds of grief into Hey nonny, nonny.
DON PEDRO. By my honor, a good song.
BALTHASAR. And a bad singer, my lord.
DON PEDRO. Ha, no, no, honestly—you sing well enough to get by.
BENEDICK.
[Aside] If he had been a dog who had howled
this way, they'd have hanged him. I pray God his bad voice doesn't forecast some mischief. I'd as soon have heard the night-raven, whatever plague might have come after it.
DON PEDRO. Yes, indeed—do you hear, Balthasar? Please, get us some excellent music, for tomorrow night we'd like it at Lady Hero's chamber window.
BALTHASAR. The best I can, my lord.
DON PEDRO. Do so. Farewell.
[Exit Balthasar and Musicians.]
Come here, Leonato. What was it you were telling me today—that your niece Beatrice was in love with Signior Benedick?
CLAUDIO. Oh, yes—[Aside to Don Pedro] Stalk on, stalk on; the bird's settled. I never thought that lady would have loved any man.
LEONATO. No, nor I either; but it's the most wonderful thing that she should dote so on Signior Benedick, whom in all her outward behavior she has always seemed to abhor.
BENEDICK.
[Aside] Is it possible? Does the wind sit in that corner?
LEONATO. Honestly, my lord, I don't know what to think of it, except that she loves him with a raging affection. It's past the infinite of thought.
DON PEDRO. Maybe she's only pretending.
CLAUDIO. Honestly, likely enough.
LEONATO. Oh God! Pretending! There was never any counterfeit of passion that came so close to the real thing as she reveals it.
DON PEDRO. Why, what effects of passion does she show?
CLAUDIO.
[Aside] Bait the hook well: this fish will bite.
LEONATO. What effects, my lord? She'll sit—[To Claudio] You heard my daughter tell you how.
CLAUDIO. She did, indeed.
DON PEDRO. How, how, please? You amaze me. I'd have thought her spirit was invincible against all assaults of affection.
LEONATO. I'd have sworn it was, my lord—especially against Benedick.
BENEDICK.
[Aside] I'd think this a hoax, except that the
white-bearded fellow says it. Trickery surely can't hide itself in such respectability.
CLAUDIO.
[Aside] He's taken the infection. Keep it
going.
DON PEDRO. Has she made her affection known to Benedick?
LEONATO. No—and she swears she never will. That's her torment.
CLAUDIO. It's true, indeed; so your daughter says: 'Shall I,' she says, 'who have so often confronted him with scorn, write to him that I love him?'

LEONATO. This is what she says now, when she's beginning to write to him; for she'll be up twenty times a night, and she'll sit there in her smock until she's written a sheet of paper. My daughter tells us everything.
CLAUDIO. Now that you mention a sheet of paper, I remember a pretty joke your daughter told us.
LEONATO. Oh! When she'd written it, and was reading it over, she found 'Benedick and Beatrice' between the sheet?
CLAUDIO. That's it.

LEONATO. Oh! She tore the letter into a thousand little pieces; railed at herself, that she should be so immodest as to write to one she knew would mock her: 'I judge him,' she says, 'by my own spirit; for I'd mock him if he wrote to me—yes, even though I love him, I would.'
CLAUDIO. Then down on her knees she falls, weeps, sobs, beats her heart, tears her hair, prays, curses: 'Oh sweet Benedick! God give me patience!'
LEONATO. She does indeed; my daughter says so; and the ecstasy has overwhelmed her so much that my daughter is sometimes afraid she'll do some desperate harm to herself. It's quite true.
DON PEDRO. It would be good if Benedick learned of it by some other means, since she won't reveal it herself.
CLAUDIO. To what end? He'd just make a sport of it and torment the poor lady worse.
DON PEDRO. If he did, it would be a kindness to hang him. She's an excellent sweet lady, and beyond all suspicion, she's virtuous.
CLAUDIO. And she's exceedingly wise.
DON PEDRO. In everything—except in loving Benedick.
LEONATO. Oh, my lord! When wisdom and passion battle in so tender a body, the odds are ten to one that passion wins. I'm sorry for her, as I've good reason to be, being her uncle and her guardian.
DON PEDRO. I wish she had bestowed this dotage on me. I'd have brushed aside all other concerns and made her half myself. Please, tell Benedick about it, and hear what he'll say.
LEONATO. Do you think it would be good?

CLAUDIO. Hero is sure she'll die; for she says she'll die if he doesn't love her, and she'll die before she makes her love known, and she'll die if he woos her, rather than abate one breath of her accustomed contrariness.
DON PEDRO. She's right: if she made an offer of her love, it's very possible he'd scorn it; for the man—as you all know—has a contemptuous spirit.
CLAUDIO. He is a very proper man.
DON PEDRO. He has a good outward appearance, yes.
CLAUDIO. Before God, and in my opinion, very wise.
DON PEDRO. He does indeed show some sparks that resemble wit.
CLAUDIO. And I take him to be brave.
DON PEDRO. Like Hector, I assure you. And in handling quarrels you might say he's wise—for either he avoids them with great discretion, or he takes them on with a most Christian-like fear.
LEONATO. If he fears God, he must necessarily keep the peace. If he breaks the peace, he ought to enter into a quarrel with fear and trembling.

DON PEDRO. And so he does; for the man does fear God, however it doesn't seem so to others, judging from some of the broad jokes he makes. Well, I'm sorry for your niece. Shall we go seek Benedick and tell him of her love?
CLAUDIO. Don't ever tell him, my lord—let her wear it out with good counsel.
LEONATO. No, that's impossible—she may wear her heart out first.
DON PEDRO. Well, we'll hear more about it from your daughter. Let it cool meanwhile. I'm fond of Benedick, and I wish he'd modestly examine himself, to see how unworthy he is of so good a lady.
LEONATO. My lord, will you walk? Dinner is ready.
CLAUDIO.
[Aside] If he doesn't dote on her after this, I'll never
trust my expectations again.
DON PEDRO.
[Aside] Let the same net be spread for her too—and

that's what your daughter and her gentlewoman must carry out. The fun will be when each holds a belief about the other's infatuation, with no such thing being real. That's the scene I'd like to see, which will be nothing but a silent show. Let's send her to call him in to dinner.
[Exit Don Pedro, Claudio and Leonato.]
BENEDICK.
[Advancing from the arbor.] This can't be a trick: the

conversation was conducted seriously. They have the truth of this from Hero. They seem to pity the lady—it seems her affections are at full stretch. Love me? Why, it must be returned. I hear how I'm being judged: they say I'll bear myself proudly, if I perceive the love coming from her; they say too that she'd rather die than give any sign of affection. I never thought to marry. I mustn't seem proud. Happy are those who hear their criticisms and can mend them. They say the lady is beautiful—that's true, I can bear them witness; and virtuous—yes, I can't deny that; and wise, except for loving me—well, honestly, that's no addition to her wit, nor any great argument of her folly, because I'm going to be horribly in love with her. I may catch some odd quirks and remnants of wit broken on me, because I've railed so long against marriage. But doesn't the appetite change? A man loves food in his youth that he can't stand in his old age. Shall quips and sayings and these paper bullets of the brain frighten a man from the course of his nature? No—the world must be peopled. When I said I'd die a bachelor, I didn't think I'd live till I was married. Here comes Beatrice. By this day! She is a beautiful lady. I do spy some marks of love in her.
[Enter Beatrice.]
BEATRICE. Against my will, I'm sent to invite you in to dinner.
BENEDICK. Fair Beatrice, I thank you for your trouble.
BEATRICE. I took no more trouble for those thanks than you take trouble to thank me. If it had been troublesome, I wouldn't have come.
BENEDICK. You take pleasure, then, in the message?
BEATRICE. Yes, just as much as you might take on the point of a knife, and choke a daw with it. You have no appetite, signior—farewell.
[Exit.]

BENEDICK. Ha! 'Against my will, I am sent to invite you in to dinner'—there's a double meaning in that. 'I took no more trouble for those thanks than you took trouble to thank me'—that's as much as to say, any trouble I take for you is as easy as thanks. If I don't take pity on her, I am a villain; if I don't love her, I am a Jew. I'll go get her picture.
[Exit.]

chapters.title: Act 3, Scene 1 — Leonato’s Garden
paragraphs: [Enter Hero, Margaret and Ursula.]

HERO. Good Margaret, run to the parlor. You'll find my cousin Beatrice there, talking with the Prince and Claudio. Whisper in her ear and tell her that Ursula and I are walking in the orchard, and our whole conversation is all about her; say you overheard us; and tell her to slip into the leafy bower where honeysuckles, ripened by the sun, forbid the sun to enter—like favorites made proud by princes, who raise their pride against the very power that fostered it. There she can hide and listen to what we propose. That's your task. Carry it out well and leave us alone.
MARGARET. I'll make her come at once, I assure you.
[Exit.]

HERO. Now, Ursula, when Beatrice arrives, as we pace this path up and down, our talk must only be of Benedick. When I mention him, your part will be to praise him beyond what any man ever deserved. My talk to you must be about how Benedick is lovesick for Beatrice. From this material is little Cupid's crafty arrow made—the kind that wounds only by hearsay.
[Enter Beatrice behind.]
Now begin. Look where Beatrice, like a lapwing, runs close by the ground to hear our conversation.

URSULA. The most pleasant angling is to see the fish cut the silver stream with her golden fins, and greedily devour the treacherous bait. So we angle for Beatrice—who even now is crouched in the woodbine cover. Don't worry about my part of the dialogue.
HERO. Then let's go nearer, so her ear loses none of the false sweet bait that we set for it.
[They advance to the bower.]
No, truly, Ursula, she is too disdainful. I know her spirits are as coy and wild as wild hawks of the cliff.
URSULA. But are you sure that Benedick loves Beatrice so entirely?
HERO. So says the Prince, and my newly-betrothed lord.
URSULA. And did they ask you to tell her of it, madam?
HERO. They begged me to acquaint her with it. But I persuaded them, if they loved Benedick, to wish him to wrestle with his affection, and never to let Beatrice know of it.
URSULA. Why did you do that? Doesn't the gentleman deserve as full and fortunate a bed as Beatrice will ever lie on?

HERO. Oh god of love! I know he does deserve as much as can be granted to any man. But Nature never fashioned a woman's heart out of prouder stuff than Beatrice's. Disdain and scorn ride sparkling in her eyes, scorning whatever they look on; and her wit values itself so highly that to her, everything else seems trivial. She cannot love, nor entertain any form or design of affection—she's so wrapped up in herself.
URSULA. Surely I think so; and therefore it would certainly not be good for her to know his love, lest she make sport of it.

HERO. Why, you speak the truth. I've never yet seen a man—however wise, however noble, young, however finely featured—but she'd interpret him backwards. If fair-faced, she'd swear the gentleman should be her sister; if dark, she'd say Nature, while drawing a clown, had made an ugly blot; if tall, a poorly-headed spear; if short, an agate very crudely carved; if talkative, a weathervane blown by every wind; if silent, a stump moved by none. So she turns every man inside out, and never gives truth and virtue what simplicity and merit deserve.
URSULA. Surely, surely, such carping isn't commendable.

HERO. No—and to be as odd and out of fashion as Beatrice is, can't be commendable either. But who dares tell her so? If I were to speak, she'd mock me into thin air; oh! she would laugh me out of myself, press me to death with wit. So let Benedick, like a covered fire, consume himself in sighs and waste away inwardly. That would be a better death than dying by mockery, which is as bad as dying by tickling.
URSULA. Yet tell her of it—hear what she'll say.

HERO. No. Rather I'll go to Benedick and counsel him to fight against his passion. And honestly, I'll devise some innocent slanders to stain my cousin with. One doesn't know how much an ill word may poison liking.
URSULA. Oh! Don't do your cousin such a wrong. She can't be so lacking in true judgment—having such a swift and excellent wit as she's prized for—as to refuse so rare a gentleman as Signior Benedick.
HERO. He's the finest man in Italy—always excepting my dear Claudio.
URSULA. Please don't be angry with me, madam, for speaking my opinion: Signior Benedick, for shape, for bearing, eloquence and valor, ranks foremost by reputation throughout Italy.
HERO. Indeed, he has an excellent good reputation.
URSULA. His excellence earned it before he had it. When do you get married, madam?
HERO. Why, any day now—tomorrow. Come, let's go inside. I'll show you some outfits and get your advice on which is best to wear tomorrow.
URSULA. She's caught, I assure you. We've caught her, madam.
HERO. If that proves true, then loving works by chances: some Cupid kills with arrows, some with traps.
[Exit Hero and Ursula.]
BEATRICE.
[Advancing.] What fire is in my ears? Can this be true?

Do I stand condemned so much for pride and scorn? Contempt, farewell! And maiden pride, adieu! No glory lives behind the back of such things. And, Benedick, love on; I will requite you, taming my wild heart to your loving hand. If you do love, my kindness shall incite you to bind our loves together in a holy band; for others say you deserve it, and I believe it more than just by hearsay.
[Exit.]

chapters.title: Act 3, Scene 2 — A Room in Leonato’s House
paragraphs: [Enter Don Pedro, Claudio, Benedick and Leonato.]
DON PEDRO. I'll only stay until your marriage is finalized, and then I'll head toward Aragon.
CLAUDIO. I'll escort you there, my lord, if you'll permit me.

DON PEDRO. No—that would be as much a stain on the fresh shine of your marriage as showing a child his new coat and then forbidding him to wear it. I'll only impose on Benedick for company, because from the crown of his head to the sole of his foot, he is all mirth. He's twice or thrice cut Cupid's bowstring, and the little hangman doesn't dare shoot at him. He has a heart as sound as a bell, and his tongue is the clapper—whatever his heart thinks, his tongue speaks.
BENEDICK. Gentlemen, I'm not as I used to be.
LEONATO. I'd say so too. You seem sadder.
CLAUDIO. I hope he's in love.
DON PEDRO. Hang him, the slacker! There isn't a true drop of blood in him to be truly touched with love. If he's sad, he just needs money.
BENEDICK. I have a toothache.
DON PEDRO. Pull it out.
BENEDICK. Hang it.
CLAUDIO. You must hang it first and draw it afterwards.
DON PEDRO. What! Sigh over a toothache?
LEONATO. Which is only a humor or a worm?
BENEDICK. Well, everyone can master a grief except the one who has it.
CLAUDIO. Yet I say he's in love.

DON PEDRO. There's no appearance of fancy in him—unless it's a fancy he has for strange disguises, like being a Dutchman today, a Frenchman tomorrow; or in the shape of two countries at once, like a German from the waist down, all loose breeches, and a Spaniard from the hip up, no doublet. Unless he has a fancy for this foolery—which it seems he does—he's no fool for fancy in the way you'd like to make him out.
CLAUDIO. If he isn't in love with some woman, there's no believing the old signs. He brushes his hat in the mornings—what should that mean?
DON PEDRO. Has anyone seen him at the barber's?
CLAUDIO. No, but the barber's man has been seen with him; and the old ornament of his cheek has already stuffed tennis balls.
LEONATO. Indeed, he looks younger than he did, with the loss of a beard.
DON PEDRO. No, he rubs himself with civet perfume—can you smell him out by that?
CLAUDIO. That's as much as to say the sweet youth's in love.
DON PEDRO. The greatest sign of it is his melancholy.
CLAUDIO. And when did he ever bother to wash his face?
DON PEDRO. Yes, or to use makeup? I hear what they say about him on that score.
CLAUDIO. No—it's his jesting spirit; which is now crept into a lute-string, and now governed by stops.
DON PEDRO. Indeed, that tells a heavy tale for him. Conclude, conclude—he's in love.
CLAUDIO. No, but I know who loves him.
DON PEDRO. I'd like to know that too—I guarantee, someone who doesn't know him.
CLAUDIO. Yes—and knows his bad qualities; and in spite of them all, dies for him.
DON PEDRO. She'll be buried with her face upwards.
BENEDICK. Yet this is no charm for the toothache. Old signior, walk aside with me—I've prepared eight or nine wise words to say to you, which these hobby-horses mustn't hear.
[Exit Benedick and Leonato.]
DON PEDRO. For my life, he's going to talk with him about Beatrice.
CLAUDIO. That's it exactly. Hero and Margaret will have played their parts with Beatrice by now, and then the two bears won't bite each other when they meet.
[Enter Don John.]
DON JOHN. My lord and brother, God save you!
DON PEDRO. Good day, brother.
DON JOHN. If your leisure permits, I'd like to speak with you.
DON PEDRO. In private?
DON JOHN. If you please—though Count Claudio may hear too, because what I'd speak about concerns him.
DON PEDRO. What's the matter?
DON JOHN.
[To Claudio.] Does your lordship mean to marry tomorrow?
DON PEDRO. You know he does.
DON JOHN. I'm not so sure he does, once he knows what I know.
CLAUDIO. If there's any impediment, please reveal it.

DON JOHN. You may think I don't love you—let that appear hereafter, and judge me better by what I'm about to disclose. As for my brother, I think he holds you in good regard, and out of dear-heartedness has helped bring about your coming marriage. Surely a suit ill-spent and labor ill-bestowed!
DON PEDRO. Why, what's the matter?
DON JOHN. I came here to tell you—and to cut a long story short, since she has been talked of too long—the lady is disloyal.
CLAUDIO. Who, Hero?
DON JOHN. The same: Leonato's Hero, your Hero, every man's Hero.
CLAUDIO. Disloyal?

DON JOHN. The word's too good to paint her wickedness. I could say she's worse—pick any worse title, and I'll fit her to it. Don't wonder until further proof. Just come with me tonight, and you'll see her chamber window entered—the very night before her wedding day. If you love her then, marry her tomorrow; but it would better suit your honor to change your mind.
CLAUDIO. Can this be so?
DON PEDRO. I won't believe it.
DON JOHN. If you dare not trust what you see, don't admit you know it. If you'll follow me, I'll show you enough; and when you've seen more and heard more, proceed accordingly.
CLAUDIO. If I see anything tonight that means I shouldn't marry her tomorrow, then in the congregation where I'd wed her, there I'll shame her.
DON PEDRO. And as I wooed in your name to win her, I'll join with you to disgrace her.
DON JOHN. I'll disparage her no further until you're my witnesses. Just stay cool until midnight, and let the outcome show itself.
DON PEDRO. Oh day untowardly turned!
CLAUDIO. Oh mischief strangely thwarting!
DON JOHN. Oh plague very well prevented! So you'll say when you've seen the sequel.
[Exit.]

chapters.title: Act 3, Scene 3 — A Street
paragraphs: [Enter Dogberry and Verges, with the Watch.]
DOGBERRY. Are you good and honest men?
VERGES. Yes, or else it would be a shame if they didn't suffer salvation, body and soul.
DOGBERRY. No, that would be too good a punishment for them, if they had any loyalty in them, being chosen for the Prince's watch.
VERGES. Well, give them their orders, neighbor Dogberry.
DOGBERRY. First, who do you think is the most deserveless man to be constable?
FIRST WATCH. Hugh Oatcake, sir, or George Seacoal—they can write and read.
DOGBERRY. Come here, neighbor Seacoal. God has blessed you with a good name. To be a good-looking man is the gift of Fortune, but writing and reading come from Nature.
SECOND WATCH. Both of which, Master Constable—

DOGBERRY. You have them. I knew that would be your answer. Well, for your good looks, sir, just thank God and don't brag about it. And for your writing and reading, save that for when there's no need of such vanity. You're thought to be the most senseless and fit man for constable of the watch, so you carry the lantern. These are your orders: you shall apprehend all vagrant men. You are to order any man to halt, in the Prince's name.
SECOND WATCH. What if he won't halt?
DOGBERRY. Why, then take no notice of him and let him go. Then call the rest of the watch together and thank God you are rid of a scoundrel.
VERGES. If he won't halt when he's ordered, he is not one of the Prince's subjects.

DOGBERRY. True, and you are not to bother with anyone but the Prince's subjects. You shall also make no noise in the streets, because for the watch to babble and talk is most tolerable and not to be endured.
SECOND WATCH. We'd rather sleep than talk. We know what belongs to a watch.

DOGBERRY. Why, you speak like an experienced and most quiet watchman, for I cannot see how sleeping should offend. Just take care that your weapons aren't stolen. Well, you are to call at all the alehouses and order the drunks to go to bed.
SECOND WATCH. What if they won't?
DOGBERRY. Why then, leave them alone until they are sober. If they don't give you a better answer then, you may say they aren't the men you took them for.
SECOND WATCH. Very well, sir.
DOGBERRY. If you meet a thief, you may suspect him, by virtue of your office, of being no honest man. And for such kinds of men, the less you bother with them, the better for your reputation.
SECOND WATCH. If we know him to be a thief, shouldn't we lay hands on him?

DOGBERRY. Truly, by your office, you may. But I think those who touch pitch will be defiled. The most peaceful course for you, if you do catch a thief, is to let him show what he is and steal away from your company.
VERGES. You have always been called a merciful man, partner.
DOGBERRY. Truly, I wouldn't hang a dog by my will, much less a man who has any honesty in him.
VERGES. If you hear a child crying in the night, you must call to the nurse and tell her to quiet it.
SECOND WATCH. What if the nurse is asleep and won't hear us?
DOGBERRY. Why then, leave in peace and let the child wake her with its crying. The ewe that will not hear her lamb when it bleats will never answer a calf when he bleats.
VERGES. That's very true.
DOGBERRY. This is the end of the orders. You, constable, are to represent the Prince's own person. If you meet the Prince in the night, you may stop him.
VERGES. No, by our Lady, I don't think he can.

DOGBERRY. Five shillings to one, with any man who knows the statutes, that he may stop him—but, indeed, not unless the Prince is willing. For the watch ought to offend no man, and it is an offense to detain a man against his will.
VERGES. By our Lady, I think that's so.
DOGBERRY. Ha, ah, ha! Well, masters, good night. If anything important happens, call me up. Keep your fellows' secrets and your own, and good night. Come, neighbor.
SECOND WATCH. Well, masters, we have our orders. Let's go sit here on the church bench until two, and then all to bed.

DOGBERRY. One more word, honest neighbors. I beg you, keep watch around Signior Leonato's door. With the wedding being there tomorrow, there's a great commotion tonight. Farewell—be vigitant, I beseech you.
[Exit Dogberry and Verges.]
[Enter Borachio and Conrade.]
BORACHIO. What, Conrade!
WATCH.
[Aside] Quiet—don't move.
BORACHIO. Conrade, I say!
CONRADE. Here, man. I'm at your elbow.
BORACHIO. By the Mass, and my elbow was itching—I thought a scab would follow.
CONRADE. I'll owe you an answer for that. Now go on with your story.
BORACHIO. Stand close beside me under this overhang, then, because it's drizzling, and I will, like a true drunkard, spill everything to you.
WATCH.
[Aside] Some treason, masters—stay close.
BORACHIO. Therefore know that I've earned a thousand ducats from Don John.
CONRADE. Is it possible that any villainy should pay so well?
BORACHIO. You should rather ask if it's possible any villainy should be so rich. Because when rich villains have need of poor ones, the poor ones can name whatever price they want.
CONRADE. I'm amazed at it.
BORACHIO. That shows you're inexperienced. You know that the fashion of a doublet, or a hat, or a cloak, is nothing to a man.
CONRADE. Yes, it's clothing.
BORACHIO. I mean the fashion.
CONRADE. Yes, the fashion is the fashion.
BORACHIO. Bah! I might as well say the fool's the fool. But don't you see what a deformed thief this fashion is?
WATCH.
[Aside] I know that Deformed—he's been a vile thief
these seven years. He goes up and down like a gentleman. I remember his name.
BORACHIO. Did you not hear someone?
CONRADE. No, it was the weathervane on the house.

BORACHIO. Don't you see, I say, what a deformed thief this fashion is? How dizzily he turns about all the hot-blooded young men between fourteen and thirty-five? Sometimes shaping them like Pharaoh's soldiers in the smoky painting, sometimes like the priests of the god Bel in the old church window, sometimes like the shaven Hercules in the smudged worm-eaten tapestry, where his codpiece looks as heavy as his club?

CONRADE. All this I see, and I see that the fashion wears out more clothing than the man. But aren't you yourself dizzy with the fashion too, that you've drifted from your story into telling me about the fashion?

BORACHIO. Not so, no—but know that tonight I've wooed Margaret, the Lady Hero's gentlewoman, under the name of Hero. She leaned out at her mistress's chamber window and bid me a thousand good nights—I'm telling this story badly. I should first tell you how the Prince, Claudio, and my master, set up and placed and convinced by my master Don John, watched from afar off in the orchard this amorous encounter.
CONRADE. And they thought Margaret was Hero?

BORACHIO. Two of them did, the Prince and Claudio. But the devil my master knew she was Margaret. Partly by his oaths, which first convinced them, partly by the dark night, which deceived them, but chiefly by my villainy, which confirmed any slander Don John had made—away went Claudio enraged. He swore he would meet her, as appointed, the next morning at the temple, and there, before the whole congregation, shame her with what he saw at night, and send her home again without a husband.
FIRST WATCH. We order you in the Prince's name—halt!
SECOND WATCH. Call up the proper Master Constable. We have here uncovered the most dangerous piece of lechery that was ever known in the commonwealth.
FIRST WATCH. And one Deformed is one of them—I know him, he wears a lock.
CONRADE. Masters, masters!
SECOND WATCH. You'll be made to bring Deformed forth, I warrant you.
CONRADE. Masters—
FIRST WATCH. Don't speak. We order you to let us obey you and go with us.
BORACHIO. We're likely to prove a fine commodity, being taken up on these men's pikes.
CONRADE. A commodity in question, I warrant you. Come, we'll obey you.
[Exit.]

chapters.title: Act 3, Scene 4 — A Room in Leonato’s House
paragraphs: [Enter Hero, Margaret and Ursula.]
HERO. Good Ursula, wake my cousin Beatrice and ask her to get up.
URSULA. I will, lady.
HERO. And tell her to come here.
URSULA. Very well.
[Exit.]
MARGARET. Honestly, I think your other collar would be better.
HERO. No, please, good Meg, I'll wear this one.
MARGARET. By my troth, it's not as good, and I guarantee your cousin will say so.
HERO. My cousin's a fool, and you're another. I'll wear nothing but this.
MARGARET. I like the new headdress inside excellently, if the hair were just a shade browner. And your gown is a most rare fashion, indeed. I saw the Duchess of Milan's gown that everyone praises so.
HERO. Oh, that one surpasses everything, they say.

MARGARET. By my troth, it's only a nightgown compared to yours: cloth of gold, with cuts, and laced with silver, set with pearls, with down sleeves, side sleeves, and skirts all around, lined underneath with a bluish tinsel—but for a fine, quaint, graceful, and excellent fashion, yours is worth ten of it.
HERO. God give me joy in wearing it, for my heart is exceedingly heavy.
MARGARET. It will be heavier soon by the weight of a man.
HERO. Shame on you! Aren't you ashamed?

MARGARET. Of what, lady? Of speaking honorably? Isn't marriage honorable even for a beggar? Isn't your lord honorable without marriage? I think you'd have me say, saving your reverence, 'a husband.' If bad thinking doesn't twist honest speaking, I'll offend no one. Is there any harm in 'heavier for a husband'? None, I think, if it be the right husband and the right wife. Otherwise it's light, and not heavy. Ask my Lady Beatrice if you don't believe me—here she comes.
[Enter Beatrice.]
HERO. Good morning, cousin.
BEATRICE. Good morning, sweet Hero.
HERO. Why, what's this? Are you speaking in the sick tone?
BEATRICE. I'm out of every other tone, it seems.
MARGARET. Strike up 'Light of Love.' That one goes without a refrain. You sing it, and I'll dance it.
BEATRICE. Yes, light of love with your heels! Then, if your husband has stables enough, you'll see he won't lack for children.
MARGARET. Oh, illegitimate construction! I scorn that with my heels.
BEATRICE. It's almost five o'clock, cousin. It's time you were ready. By my troth, I am exceedingly ill. Heigh-ho!
MARGARET. For a hawk, a horse, or a husband?
BEATRICE. For the letter that begins them all—H.
MARGARET. Well, if you haven't turned Turk, then there's no more sailing by the stars.
BEATRICE. What does this fool mean, I wonder?
MARGARET. Nothing, I—but God send everyone their heart's desire!
HERO. These gloves the Count sent me—they have an excellent perfume.
BEATRICE. I'm stuffed up, cousin, I cannot smell.
MARGARET. A maid, and stuffed! There's a fine catching of cold.
BEATRICE. Oh, God help me, God help me! How long have you been professing wit?
MARGARET. Ever since you gave it up. Doesn't my wit suit me marvelously?
BEATRICE. It isn't seen enough—you should wear it in your cap. By my troth, I am sick.
MARGARET. Get yourself some of this distilled Carduus benedictus, and apply it to your heart. It's the only thing for a sickly turn.
HERO. There you prick her with a thistle.
BEATRICE. Benedictus! Why benedictus? You have some hidden meaning in this benedictus.

MARGARET. Meaning! No, by my troth, I have no hidden meaning. I meant just plain holy thistle. You may think, perhaps, that I think you're in love. No, by our Lady, I am not such a fool as to think whatever I please; nor do I please to think whatever I can; nor, indeed, can I think, if I would think my heart out of thinking, that you are in love, or that you will be in love, or that you can be in love. Yet Benedick was just the same, and now he's become a man. He swore he would never marry, and yet now, despite his heart, he eats his meat without grudging. And how you may be converted, I don't know—but I think you look out of your eyes as other women do.
BEATRICE. What pace is this that your tongue keeps?
MARGARET. Not a false gallop.
[Re-enter Ursula.]
URSULA. Madam, withdraw—the Prince, the Count, Signior Benedick, Don John, and all the gallants of the town have come to fetch you to church.
HERO. Help dress me, good cousin, good Meg, good Ursula.
[Exit.]

chapters.title: Act 3, Scene 5 — Another Room in Leonato’s House
paragraphs: [Enter Leonato and Dogberry and Verges.]
LEONATO. What do you want with me, honest neighbor?
DOGBERRY. By the Mass, sir, I would have some confidence with you, that decerns you nearly.
LEONATO. Make it brief, I pray you, for you see this is a busy time for me.
DOGBERRY. By the Mass, this is it, sir.
VERGES. Yes, in truth it is, sir.
LEONATO. What is it, my good friends?

DOGBERRY. Goodman Verges, sir, speaks a little off the point: an old man, sir, and his wits aren't as sharp as, God help us, I would wish they were; but, in faith, as honest as the skin between his brows.
VERGES. Yes, I thank God, I am as honest as any man living, that is an old man and no more honest than I am.
DOGBERRY. Comparisons are odorous: palabras, neighbor Verges.
LEONATO. Neighbors, you are tedious.

DOGBERRY. It pleases your worship to say so, but we are the poor Duke's officers. But truly, for my own part, if I were as tedious as a king, I could find it in my heart to bestow it all on your worship.
LEONATO. All your tediousness on me, eh?
DOGBERRY. Yes, and if it were a thousand pound more than it is. For I hear as good a report of your worship as of any man in the city, and though I be but a poor man, I am glad to hear it.
VERGES. And so am I.
LEONATO. I would gladly know what you have to say.
VERGES. By the Mass, sir, our watch tonight, saving your worship's presence, has taken a couple of as utter scoundrels as any in Messina.

DOGBERRY. A good old man, sir; he will be talking. As they say, 'When the age is in, the wit is out.' God help us, it's a world to see! Well said, in faith, neighbor Verges. Well, God's a good man; and when two men ride on a horse, one must ride behind. An honest soul, in faith, sir; by my troth he is, as ever broke bread. But God is to be worshipped: all men are not alike; alas, good neighbor!
LEONATO. Indeed, neighbor, he comes too short of you.
DOGBERRY. Gifts that God gives.
LEONATO. I must leave you.
DOGBERRY. One word, sir: our watch, sir, has indeed apprehended two aspicious persons, and we would have them examined before your worship this morning.
LEONATO. Take their examination yourselves, and bring it to me. I am now in great haste, as may be apparent to you.
DOGBERRY. It shall be suffigance.
LEONATO. Drink some wine before you go. Fare you well.
[Enter a Messenger.]
MESSENGER. My lord, they're waiting for you to give your daughter to her husband.
LEONATO. I'll attend them. I am ready.
[Exit Leonato and Messenger.]
DOGBERRY. Go, good partner, go get yourself to Francis Seacoal. Tell him to bring his pen and inkhorn to the jail. We are now to examination these men.
VERGES. And we must do it wisely.
DOGBERRY. We will spare for no wit, I warrant you. Here's that which shall drive some of them to a non-come. Only get the learned writer to set down our excommunication, and meet me at the jail.
[Exit.]

chapters.title: Act 4, Scene 1 — The Inside of a Church
paragraphs: [Enter Don Pedro, Don John, Leonato, Friar Francis, Claudio, Benedick, Hero, Beatrice, etc.]
LEONATO. Come, Friar Francis, be brief—just the plain form of marriage, and you can recount their particular duties afterward.
FRIAR. You come here, my lord, to marry this lady?
CLAUDIO. No.
LEONATO. To be married to her, friar; you come to marry her.
FRIAR. Lady, you come here to be married to this Count?
HERO. I do.
FRIAR. If either of you knows any inward impediment why you should not be joined, I charge you, on your souls, to speak it.
CLAUDIO. Do you know any, Hero?
HERO. None, my lord.
FRIAR. Do you know any, Count?
LEONATO. I dare answer for him—none.
CLAUDIO. Oh, what men dare do! What men may do! What men daily do, not knowing what they do!
BENEDICK. What's this? Interjections? Why then, some are of laughter, as ah! ha! he!
CLAUDIO. Stand aside, Friar. Father, by your leave: will you, with free and unconstrained soul, give me this maid, your daughter?
LEONATO. As freely, son, as God gave her to me.
CLAUDIO. And what have I to give back to you whose worth may counter-balance this rich and precious gift?
DON PEDRO. Nothing, unless you return her again.

CLAUDIO. Sweet Prince, you teach me noble thankfulness. There, Leonato—take her back again. Don't give this rotten orange to your friend. She is only the sign and semblance of her honor. Behold how like a maid she blushes here! Oh, with what authority and show of truth can cunning sin cover itself! Doesn't that blood come as modest evidence to witness simple virtue? Wouldn't you all swear, you who see her, that she were a maid, by these outward signs? But she is no maid. She knows the heat of a lustful bed. Her blush is guilt, not modesty.
LEONATO. What do you mean, my lord?
CLAUDIO. Not to be married. Not to bind my soul to a proven wanton.
LEONATO. Dear my lord, if you, by your own proving, have vanquished the resistance of her youth and broken her virginity—

CLAUDIO. I know what you would say: if I have known her, you will say she embraced me as a husband, and so excuse the sin before marriage. No, Leonato—I never tempted her with any word too forward; but as a brother to his sister, I showed bashful sincerity and seemly love.
HERO. And did I ever seem otherwise to you?

CLAUDIO. Out on you! Seeming! I will write against it. You seem to me as Diana in her sphere, as chaste as the bud before it is bloomed; but you are more uncontrolled in your blood than Venus, or those pampered animals that rage in savage sensuality.
HERO. Is my lord well, that he speaks so wildly?
LEONATO. Sweet Prince, why don't you speak?
DON PEDRO. What should I say? I stand dishonored, that I went about to link my dear friend to a common harlot.
LEONATO. Are these things spoken, or do I only dream?
DON JOHN. Sir, they are spoken, and these things are true.
BENEDICK. This does not look like a wedding.
HERO. True! O God!
CLAUDIO. Leonato, do I stand here? Is this the Prince? Is this the Prince's brother? Is this face Hero's? Are our eyes our own?
LEONATO. All this is so; but what of this, my lord?
CLAUDIO. Let me only put one question to your daughter, and by that fatherly and kindly power that you have over her, bid her answer truly.
LEONATO. I charge you to do so, as you are my child.
HERO. Oh, God defend me! How am I beset! What kind of catechizing do you call this?
CLAUDIO. To make you answer truly to your name.
HERO. Is it not Hero? Who can stain that name with any just reproach?

CLAUDIO. By the Mass, Hero herself can—Hero herself can blot out Hero's virtue. What man was that I saw talking with you last night out at your window, between twelve and one? Now, if you are a maid, answer to this.
HERO. I talked with no man at that hour, my lord.

DON PEDRO. Why then you are no maiden. Leonato, I am sorry you must hear this: upon my honor, myself, my brother, and this grieved Count, did see her, hear her, at that hour last night, talk with a ruffian at her chamber window—who has, indeed, like a free-spoken villain, confessed the vile encounters they have had a thousand times in secret.

DON JOHN. Fie, fie! They are not to be named, my lord, not to be spoken of. There is not chastity enough in language to utter them without offense. Thus, pretty lady, I am sorry for your much misconduct.
