CLAUDIO. Oh Hero! What a Hero you would have been, if half your outward graces had been placed about your thoughts and the counsels of your heart! But farewell, most foul, most fair! Farewell, you pure impiety and impious purity! For you I'll lock up all the gates of love, and on my eyelids suspicion shall hang, to turn all beauty into thoughts of harm, and never shall it more be gracious.
LEONATO. Hasn't any man's dagger here a point for me?
[Hero swoons.]
BEATRICE. What's this, cousin! Why do you sink down?
DON JOHN. Come, let us go. These things, brought thus to light, smother her spirits.
[Exit Don Pedro, Don John, and Claudio.]
BENEDICK. How does the lady?
BEATRICE. Dead, I think! Help, uncle! Hero! Why, Hero! Uncle! Signior Benedick! Friar!
LEONATO. O Fate! Don't take away your heavy hand. Death is the fairest cover for her shame that could be wished for.
BEATRICE. How now, cousin Hero?
FRIAR. Take comfort, lady.
LEONATO. Are you looking up?
FRIAR. Yes; why shouldn't she?

LEONATO. Why? Doesn't every earthly thing cry shame upon her? Could she here deny the story that is printed in her blood? Don't live, Hero; don't open your eyes. For, if I thought you would not quickly die, if I thought your spirits were stronger than your shame, I myself, after these reproaches, would strike at your life. Did I grieve I had only one? Did I chide frugal Nature's design for that? Oh, one too many by you. Why did I have one? Why were you ever lovely in my eyes? Why didn't I, with charitable hand, take up a beggar's child at my gates, who, smeared like this and mired with infamy, I might have said, 'No part of it is mine; this shame derives itself from unknown loins'? But mine, and mine I loved, and mine I praised, and mine I was proud of, mine so much that I myself, to myself, was not mine, valuing her; why, she—oh, she is fallen into a pit of ink, that the wide sea has too few drops to wash her clean again, and salt too little to season her foul tainted flesh.
BENEDICK. Sir, sir, be patient. For my part, I am so dressed in wonder, I do not know what to say.
BEATRICE. Oh, upon my soul, my cousin is slandered!
BENEDICK. Lady, were you her bedfellow last night?
BEATRICE. No, truly, not—although, until last night, I have for the past twelve months been her bedfellow.

LEONATO. Confirmed, confirmed! Oh, that is made stronger which was before barred up with ribs of iron. Would the two princes lie? And Claudio lie, who loved her so that, in speaking of her foulness, he washed it with tears? Away from her! Let her die.

FRIAR. Hear me a little. I have only been silent so long, and given way to this course of events, by observing the lady. I have noted a thousand blushing apparitions start into her face; a thousand innocent shames, in angelic whiteness, bear away those blushes. And in her eye there has appeared a fire to burn the errors that these princes hold against her maiden truth. Call me a fool; trust not my reading nor my observations, which with experimental seal warrant the substance of my book; trust not my age, my reverence, my calling, nor my divinity—if this sweet lady does not lie here guiltless, under some biting error.

LEONATO. Friar, it cannot be. You see that all the grace she has left is that she will not add to her damnation the sin of perjury: she does not deny it. Why then do you seek to cover with excuse what appears in proper nakedness?
FRIAR. Lady, what man is he that you are accused of?

HERO. They know, who accuse me; I know none. If I know more of any man alive than what maiden modesty warrants, let all my sins lack mercy! O, my father! Prove that any man with me has conversed at unfit hours, or that I last night exchanged words with any creature, then reject me, hate me, torture me to death.
FRIAR. There is some strange misunderstanding in the princes.
BENEDICK. Two of them have the very bent of honor; and if their wisdoms are misled in this, the practice of it lives in John the bastard, whose spirits toil in framing villainies.

LEONATO. I do not know. If they speak only the truth of her, these hands shall tear her; if they wrong her honor, the proudest of them shall well hear of it. Time has not yet so dried this blood of mine, nor age so eaten up my invention, nor fortune made such havoc of my means, nor my bad life robbed me of so many friends, but they shall find, awakened in such a cause, both strength of limb and policy of mind, ability in means and choice of friends, to repay them in full.

FRIAR. Pause a while, and let my counsel sway you in this case. Your daughter here the princes left for dead. Let her for a while be secretly kept hidden, and publish it that she is dead indeed. Maintain a show of mourning, and on your family's old monument hang mournful epitaphs and do all the rites that belong to a burial.
LEONATO. What shall come of this? What will this do?

FRIAR. By the Mass, this well carried shall on her behalf change slander into remorse; that is some good. But it is not for that reason I dream up this strange course—but on this labor I look for greater birth. She dying, as it must be maintained, upon the instant she was accused, shall be lamented, pitied, and excused by every hearer. For so it falls out: that what we have, we don't prize at its worth while we enjoy it; but being lacked and lost, why, then we exaggerate the value, then we find the virtue that possession would not show us while it was ours. So will it be with Claudio: when he shall hear she died upon his words, the idea of her life shall sweetly creep into the study of his imagination, and every lovely organ of her life shall come dressed in more precious habit, more moving, delicate, and full of life, into the eye and prospect of his soul, than when she lived indeed. Then shall he mourn—if ever love had any interest in his liver—and wish he had not so accused her, no, even though he thought his accusation true. Let this be so, and doubt not but success will fashion the event in better shape than I can lay it down in likelihood. But if everything else is aimed falsely, the supposition of the lady's death will quench the wonder of her infamy. And if it does not sort well, you may conceal her—as best befits her wounded reputation—in some reclusive and religious life, out of all eyes, tongues, minds, and injuries.

BENEDICK. Signior Leonato, let the friar advise you. And though you know my closeness and love is very much given to the Prince and Claudio, yet, by my honor, I will deal in this as secretly and justly as your soul should with your body.
LEONATO. Since I am flowing in grief, the smallest thread may lead me.
FRIAR. It is well agreed. Away at once; for strange wounds need strange cures. Come, lady, die to live: this wedding day perhaps is only postponed. Have patience and endure.
[Exit Friar, Hero, and Leonato.]
BENEDICK. Lady Beatrice, have you wept all this while?
BEATRICE. Yes, and I will weep a while longer.
BENEDICK. I do not want you to.
BEATRICE. You have no reason; I do it freely.
BENEDICK. Surely I believe your fair cousin is wronged.
BEATRICE. Ah, how much might the man deserve of me who would right her!
BENEDICK. Is there any way to show such friendship?
BEATRICE. A very clear way, but no such friend.
BENEDICK. May a man do it?
BEATRICE. It is a man's office, but not yours.
BENEDICK. I love nothing in the world so well as you. Isn't that strange?

BEATRICE. As strange as the thing I do not know. It would be just as possible for me to say I loved nothing so well as you—but don't believe me, and yet I do not lie. I confess nothing, nor do I deny anything. I am sorry for my cousin.
BENEDICK. By my sword, Beatrice, you love me.
BEATRICE. Don't swear by it, and eat it.
BENEDICK. I will swear by it that you love me, and I will make him eat it that says I love not you.
BEATRICE. Will you not eat your word?
BENEDICK. With no sauce that can be devised for it. I declare I love you.
BEATRICE. Why then, God forgive me!
BENEDICK. What offense, sweet Beatrice?
BEATRICE. You stopped me in a happy hour: I was about to declare I loved you.
BENEDICK. And do it with all your heart.
BEATRICE. I love you with so much of my heart that none is left to declare it.
BENEDICK. Come, bid me do anything for you.
BEATRICE. Kill Claudio.
BENEDICK. Ha! Not for the wide world.
BEATRICE. You kill me to deny it. Farewell.
BENEDICK. Wait, sweet Beatrice.
BEATRICE. I am gone, though I am here. There is no love in you. No, I pray you, let me go.
BENEDICK. Beatrice—
BEATRICE. In faith, I will go.
BENEDICK. We'll be friends first.
BEATRICE. You'd more easily be friends with me than fight with my enemy.
BENEDICK. Is Claudio your enemy?

BEATRICE. Hasn't he proved himself thoroughly a villain, who has slandered, scorned, dishonored my kinswoman? Oh, that I were a man! What! Lead her on until they come to take hands, and then, with public accusation, open slander, unmitigated rancor—O God, that I were a man! I would eat his heart in the marketplace.
BENEDICK. Hear me, Beatrice—
BEATRICE. Talk with a man out at a window! A pretty saying!
BENEDICK. No, but Beatrice—
BEATRICE. Sweet Hero! She is wronged, she is slandered, she is undone.
BENEDICK. Beat—

BEATRICE. Princes and Counts! Surely, a princely testimony, a fine Count Sugar-Candy; a sweet gallant, surely! Oh, that I were a man for his sake, or that I had any friend who would be a man for my sake! But manhood is melted into curtsies, valor into compliment, and men are only turned into tongue, and trim ones too: he is now as valiant as Hercules who only tells a lie and swears it. I cannot be a man by wishing, therefore I will die a woman with grieving.
BENEDICK. Wait, good Beatrice. By this hand, I love you.
BEATRICE. Use it for my love some other way than swearing by it.
BENEDICK. Do you think in your soul that the Count Claudio has wronged Hero?
BEATRICE. Yes, as sure as I have a thought or a soul.

BENEDICK. Enough! I am engaged, I will challenge him. I will kiss your hand, and so leave you. By this hand, Claudio shall render me a dear account. As you hear of me, so think of me. Go, comfort your cousin. I must say she is dead; and so, farewell.
[Exit.]

chapters.title: Act 4, Scene 2 — A Prison
paragraphs: [Enter Dogberry, Verges, and Sexton, in gowns; and the Watch, with Conrade and Borachio.]
DOGBERRY. Is our whole dissembly assembled?
VERGES. Oh, a stool and a cushion for the sexton.
SEXTON. Which are the malefactors?
DOGBERRY. By the Mass, that's me and my partner.
VERGES. No, that's certain: we have the exhibition to examine.
SEXTON. But which are the offenders who are to be examined? Let them come before Master Constable.
DOGBERRY. Yes, by the Mass, let them come before me. What is your name, friend?
BORACHIO. Borachio.
DOGBERRY. Please write down Borachio. Yours, sirrah?
CONRADE. I am a gentleman, sir, and my name is Conrade.
DOGBERRY. Write down Master gentleman Conrade. Masters, do you serve God?
BOTH. Yes, sir, we hope so.

DOGBERRY. Write down that they hope they serve God—and write God first; for God forbid that God should walk behind such villains! Masters, it is proved already that you are little better than false scoundrels, and it will go near to be thought so shortly. How do you answer for yourselves?
CONRADE. By the Mass, sir, we say we are none.
DOGBERRY. A marvelously witty fellow, I assure you—but I will get around him. Come here, sirrah: a word in your ear. Sir, I tell you, it is thought you are false scoundrels.
BORACHIO. Sir, I tell you we are none.
DOGBERRY. Well, stand aside. Before God, they are both telling the same story. Have you written down that they are none?
SEXTON. Master Constable, you are not going the right way to examine. You must call forth the watch who are their accusers.
DOGBERRY. Yes, by the Mass, that's the eftest way. Let the watch come forth. Masters, I charge you, in the Prince's name, accuse these men.
FIRST WATCH. This man said, sir, that Don John, the Prince's brother, was a villain.
DOGBERRY. Write down Prince John a villain. Why, this is flat perjury, to call a Prince's brother a villain.
BORACHIO. Master Constable—
DOGBERRY. I pray you, fellow, be quiet. I do not like your look, I promise you.
SEXTON. What else did you hear him say?
SECOND WATCH. By the Mass, that he had received a thousand ducats from Don John for accusing the Lady Hero wrongfully.
DOGBERRY. Flat burglary as was ever committed.
VERGES. Yes, by the Mass, that it is.
SEXTON. What else, fellow?
FIRST WATCH. And that Count Claudio meant, upon his words, to disgrace Hero before the whole assembly, and not marry her.
DOGBERRY. Oh villain! You will be condemned into everlasting redemption for this.
SEXTON. What else?
SECOND WATCH. This is all.

SEXTON. And this is more, masters, than you can deny. Prince John has this morning secretly fled. Hero was in this manner accused, in this manner rejected, and, upon the grief of this, suddenly died. Master Constable, let these men be bound and brought to Leonato's house. I will go ahead and show him their examination.
[Exit.]
DOGBERRY. Come, let them be opinioned.
VERGES. Let them be in the hands—
CONRADE. Off, coxcomb!
DOGBERRY. God's my life! Where's the sexton? Let him write down the Prince's officer coxcomb. Come, bind them. You naughty varlet!
CONRADE. Away! You are an ass; you are an ass.

DOGBERRY. Don't you respect my position? Don't you respect my years? Oh, that he were here to write me down an ass! But, masters, remember that I am an ass. Though it be not written down, yet forget not that I am an ass. No, you villain, you are full of piety, as shall be proved upon you by good witness. I am a wise fellow; and, which is more, an officer; and, which is more, a householder; and, which is more, as pretty a piece of flesh as any in Messina; and one that knows the law, go to; and a rich fellow enough, go to; and a fellow that has had losses; and one that has two gowns, and everything handsome about him. Bring him away. Oh, that I had been written down an ass!
[Exit.]

chapters.title: Act 5, Scene 1 — Before Leonato’s House
paragraphs: [Enter Leonato and Antonio.]
ANTONIO. If you go on like this, you'll kill yourself. And it's not wisdom to thus second grief against yourself.

LEONATO. I pray you, stop your counsel, which falls into my ears as useless as water in a sieve. Don't give me counsel; nor let any comforter please my ear except such a one whose wrongs match mine. Bring me a father who so loved his child, whose joy of her is overwhelmed like mine, and bid him speak of patience. Measure his woe the length and breadth of mine, and let it answer every strain for strain, as thus for thus and such a grief for such, in every lineament, branch, shape, and form. If such a one will smile and stroke his beard, bid sorrow be off, cry 'hem' when he should groan, patch grief with proverbs, make misfortune drunk with bookworm philosophers—bring him then to me, and from him I will gather patience. But there is no such man. For, brother, men can counsel and speak comfort to that grief which they themselves do not feel; but, tasting it, their counsel turns to passion, which before would give medicinal precepts to rage, fetter strong madness in a silken thread, charm ache with air and agony with words. No, no; it is every man's office to speak patience to those that writhe under the load of sorrow, but no man's virtue nor sufficiency to be so moral when he himself shall endure the like. Therefore give me no counsel. My griefs cry louder than admonishment.
ANTONIO. In that, men differ nothing from children.

LEONATO. I pray you, peace! I will be flesh and blood. For there was never yet a philosopher who could endure the toothache patiently, however they have written in the style of gods and made light of chance and suffering.
ANTONIO. Yet don't turn all the harm upon yourself. Make those that have offended you suffer too.
LEONATO. There you speak reason: no, I will do so. My soul tells me Hero is slandered; and that Claudio shall know; so shall the Prince, and all of them that thus dishonor her.
ANTONIO. Here comes the Prince and Claudio in haste.
[Enter Don Pedro and Claudio.]
DON PEDRO. Good day, good day.
CLAUDIO. Good day to both of you.
LEONATO. Hear me, my lords—
DON PEDRO. We are in some haste, Leonato.
LEONATO. In some haste, my lord! Well, fare you well, my lord. Are you so hasty now? Well, all is one.
DON PEDRO. No, do not quarrel with us, good old man.
ANTONIO. If he could right himself by quarreling, some of us would lie low.
CLAUDIO. Who wrongs him?
LEONATO. By the Mass, you do wrong me—you dissembler, you. No, never lay your hand upon your sword. I fear you not.
CLAUDIO. By the Mass, beshrew my hand, if it should give your age such cause of fear. In faith, my hand meant nothing toward my sword.

LEONATO. Tush, tush, man! Never sneer and jest at me. I do not speak like a dotard or a fool, as, under the privilege of age, to brag what I have done being young, or what I would do, were I not old. Know, Claudio, to your face, you have so wronged my innocent child and me, that I am forced to lay my dignity aside, and, with grey hairs and the bruises of many days, do challenge you to single combat. I say you have slandered my innocent child. Your slander has gone through and through her heart, and she lies buried with her ancestors—oh, in a tomb where scandal never slept, save this of hers, framed by your villainy!
CLAUDIO. My villainy?
LEONATO. Yours, Claudio; yours, I say.
DON PEDRO. You do not say right, old man.
LEONATO. My lord, my lord, I'll prove it on his body if he dares, despite his fine fencing and his active practice, his May of youth and bloom of vigor.
CLAUDIO. Away! I will not have anything to do with you.
LEONATO. Can you so brush me off? You have killed my child. If you kill me, boy, you shall kill a man.

ANTONIO. He shall kill two of us, and men indeed. But that's no matter; let him kill one first. Win me and wear me; let him answer me. Come, follow me, boy; come, sir boy, come, follow me. Sir boy, I'll whip you out of your thrusting fence. No, as I am a gentleman, I will.
LEONATO. Brother—

ANTONIO. Be content. God knows I loved my niece, and she is dead, slandered to death by villains, that dare as much answer a man indeed as I dare take a serpent by the tongue. Boys, apes, braggarts, Jacks, milksops!
LEONATO. Brother Antonio—

ANTONIO. Hold yourself content. What, man! I know them, yes, and what they weigh, even to the utmost scruple—scrambling, brazen, fashion-mongering boys, that lie and cheat and flout, deprave and slander, dress fantastically, show outward hideousness, and speak off half a dozen dangerous words about how they might hurt their enemies if they dared—and this is all!
LEONATO. But, brother Antonio—
ANTONIO. Come, it's no matter. Don't you meddle, let me deal with this.
DON PEDRO. Gentlemen both, we will not wake your patience. My heart is sorry for your daughter's death; but, on my honor, she was charged with nothing but what was true and very full of proof.
LEONATO. My lord, my lord—
DON PEDRO. I will not hear you.
LEONATO. No? Come, brother, away. I will be heard.—
ANTONIO. And shall, or some of us will smart for it.
[Exit Leonato and Antonio.]
[Enter Benedick.]
DON PEDRO. See, see; here comes the man we went to seek.
CLAUDIO. Now, signior, what news?
BENEDICK. Good day, my lord.
DON PEDRO. Welcome, signior. You are almost come in time to part almost a fray.
CLAUDIO. We nearly had our two noses snapped off by two old men without teeth.
DON PEDRO. Leonato and his brother. What do you think? Had we fought, I doubt we would have been too young for them.
BENEDICK. In a false quarrel there is no true valor. I came to seek you both.
CLAUDIO. We have been up and down looking for you, for we are high-proof melancholy, and would gladly have it beaten away. Will you use your wit?
BENEDICK. It is in my scabbard; shall I draw it?
DON PEDRO. Do you wear your wit at your side?
CLAUDIO. No one ever did so, though very many have been beside their wit. I will bid you draw, as we do the minstrels; draw, to give us pleasure.
DON PEDRO. As I am an honest man, he looks pale. Are you sick, or angry?
CLAUDIO. What, courage, man! What though care killed a cat, you have mettle enough in you to kill care.
BENEDICK. Sir, I shall meet your wit in the career, if you charge it against me. I pray you, choose another subject.
CLAUDIO. No, then, give him another staff: this last was broken crosswise.
DON PEDRO. By this light, he changes more and more. I think he is angry indeed.
CLAUDIO. If he is, he knows how to turn his girdle.
BENEDICK. Shall I speak a word in your ear?
CLAUDIO. God bless me from a challenge!
BENEDICK.
[Aside to Claudio.] You are a villain, I do not jest. I will

make it good however you dare, with whatever you dare, and whenever you dare. Do me right, or I will declare your cowardice. You have killed a sweet lady, and her death shall fall heavy on you. Let me hear from you.
CLAUDIO. Well, I will meet you, so I may have good cheer.
DON PEDRO. What, a feast, a feast?
CLAUDIO. In faith, I thank him; he has invited me to a calf's-head and a capon, the which if I do not carve most curiously, say my knife's no good. Shall I not find a woodcock too?
BENEDICK. Sir, your wit ambles well; it goes easily.

DON PEDRO. I'll tell you how Beatrice praised your wit the other day. I said, you had a fine wit. 'True,' says she, 'a fine little one.' 'No,' said I, 'a great wit.' 'Right,' said she, 'a great gross one.' 'No,' said I, 'a good wit.' 'Just so,' said she, 'it hurts nobody.' 'No,' said I, 'the gentleman is wise.' 'Certain,' said she, 'a wise gentleman.' 'No,' said I, 'he has the tongues.' 'That I believe,' said she, 'for he swore a thing to me on Monday night, which he forswore on Tuesday morning—there's a double tongue; there's two tongues.' Thus did she, for an hour together, trans-shape your particular virtues; yet at last she concluded with a sigh, you were the properest man in Italy.
CLAUDIO. For which she wept heartily and said she did not care.
DON PEDRO. Yes, that she did; but yet, for all that, if she did not hate him deadly, she would love him dearly. The old man's daughter told us all.
CLAUDIO. All, all; and moreover, God saw him when he was hid in the garden.
DON PEDRO. But when shall we set the savage bull's horns on the sensible Benedick's head?
CLAUDIO. Yes, and text underneath, 'Here dwells Benedick the married man!'

BENEDICK. Fare you well, boy. You know my mind. I will leave you now to your gossip-like humor. You break jests as braggarts do their blades, which, God be thanked, hurt not. My lord, for your many courtesies I thank you. I must discontinue your company. Your brother the bastard has fled from Messina. You have, among you, killed a sweet and innocent lady. As for my Lord Lack-beard there, he and I shall meet; and till then, peace be with him.
[Exit.]
DON PEDRO. He is in earnest.
CLAUDIO. In most profound earnest; and, I'll warrant you, for the love of Beatrice.
DON PEDRO. And has challenged you?
CLAUDIO. Most sincerely.
DON PEDRO. What a pretty thing man is when he goes in his doublet and hose and leaves off his wit!
CLAUDIO. He is then a giant to an ape; but then an ape is a doctor to such a man.
DON PEDRO. But, hold; let me be. Pluck up, my heart, and be sad! Didn't he say my brother had fled?
[Enter Dogberry, Verges, and the Watch, with Conrade and Borachio.]
DOGBERRY. Come on, sir: if justice cannot tame you, she shall never weigh more reasons in her balance. No, if you are a cursing hypocrite once, you must be looked to.
DON PEDRO. What's this? Two of my brother's men bound! Borachio, one of them!
CLAUDIO. Hear about their offense, my lord.
DON PEDRO. Officers, what offense have these men done?

DOGBERRY. By the Mass, sir, they have committed false report; moreover, they have spoken untruths; secondarily, they are slanders; sixth and lastly, they have slandered a lady; thirdly, they have verified unjust things; and to conclude, they are lying scoundrels.
DON PEDRO. First, I ask you what they have done; thirdly, I ask you what's their offense; sixth and lastly, why they are committed; and, to conclude, what you lay to their charge?
CLAUDIO. Rightly reasoned, and in his own division; and, by my troth, there's one meaning well dressed up.
DON PEDRO. Whom have you offended, masters, that you are thus bound to answer? This learned constable is too cunning to be understood. What's your offense?

BORACHIO. Sweet Prince, let me go no further in my answer. Hear me, and let this Count kill me. I have deceived even your very eyes: what your wisdoms could not discover, these shallow fools have brought to light. In the night, they overheard me confessing to this man how Don John your brother incited me to slander the Lady Hero; how you were brought into the orchard and saw me court Margaret in Hero's clothes; how you disgraced her when you should have married her. My villainy they have on record—which I had rather seal with my death than repeat over to my shame. The lady is dead upon my and my master's false accusation; and, briefly, I desire nothing but the reward of a villain.
DON PEDRO. Doesn't this speech run like iron through your blood?
CLAUDIO. I have drunk poison while he uttered it.
DON PEDRO. But did my brother set you on to this?
BORACHIO. Yes; and paid me richly for the practice of it.
DON PEDRO. He is composed and framed of treachery. And he has fled upon this villainy.
CLAUDIO. Sweet Hero! Now your image does appear in the rare semblance that I loved it first.

DOGBERRY. Come, bring away the plaintiffs. By this time our sexton has informed Signior Leonato of the matter. And masters, do not forget to specify, when time and place shall serve, that I am an ass.
VERGES. Here, here comes Master Signior Leonato, and the sexton too.
[Re-enter Leonato, Antonio, and the Sexton.]
LEONATO. Which is the villain? Let me see his eyes, so that, when I note another man like him, I may avoid him. Which of these is he?
BORACHIO. If you would know who wronged you, look on me.
LEONATO. Are you the slave who, with your breath, has killed my innocent child?
BORACHIO. Yes, even I alone.

LEONATO. No, not so, villain. You slander yourself. Here stand a pair of honorable men; a third is fled, who had a hand in it. I thank you, princes, for my daughter's death. Record it with your high and worthy deeds. It was bravely done, if you think about it.

CLAUDIO. I do not know how to plead for your patience; yet I must speak. Choose your revenge yourself. Impose me to whatever penance your invention can lay upon my sin—yet I sinned not but in mistaking.
DON PEDRO. By my soul, nor I. And yet, to satisfy this good old man, I would bend under any heavy weight that he'll enjoin me to.

LEONATO. I cannot bid you bid my daughter live—that were impossible; but, I pray you both, inform the people of Messina here how innocently she died. And if your love can labor anything in sad invention, hang an epitaph upon her tomb, and sing it to her bones—sing it tonight. Tomorrow morning come to my house, and since you could not be my son-in-law, be yet my nephew. My brother has a daughter, almost the copy of my child that's dead, and she alone is heir to both of us. Give her the right you should have given her cousin, and so dies my revenge.
CLAUDIO. O noble sir, your over-kindness wrings tears from me! I do embrace your offer; and dispose henceforth of poor Claudio.

LEONATO. Tomorrow then I will expect your coming. Tonight I take my leave. This naughty man shall face to face be brought to Margaret, who, I believe, was packed in all this wrong, hired to it by your brother.
BORACHIO. No, by my soul she was not; nor knew what she did when she spoke to me; but always has been just and virtuous in anything that I do know by her.

DOGBERRY. Moreover, sir—which, indeed, is not under white and black—this plaintiff here, the offender, did call me ass. I beseech you, let it be remembered in his punishment. And also, the watch heard them talk of one Deformed. They say he wears a key in his ear and a lock hanging by it, and borrows money in God's name, the which he has used so long and never paid, that now men grow hard-hearted, and will lend nothing for God's sake. Pray you, examine him upon that point.
LEONATO. I thank you for your care and honest pains.
DOGBERRY. Your worship speaks like a most thankful and reverent youth, and I praise God for you.
LEONATO. There's for your pains.
DOGBERRY. God save the foundation!
LEONATO. Go, I discharge you of your prisoner, and I thank you.

DOGBERRY. I leave an arrant scoundrel with your worship, which I beseech your worship to correct yourself, for the example of others. God keep your worship! I wish your worship well; God restore you to health! I humbly give you leave to depart, and if a merry meeting may be wished, God prohibit it! Come, neighbor.
[Exit Dogberry and Verges.]
LEONATO. Until tomorrow morning, lords, farewell.
ANTONIO. Farewell, my lords. We look for you tomorrow.
DON PEDRO. We will not fail.
CLAUDIO. Tonight I'll mourn with Hero.
[Exit Don Pedro and Claudio.]
LEONATO.
[To the Watch.] Bring these fellows on. We'll talk with
Margaret, how her acquaintance grew with this lewd fellow.
[Exit.]

chapters.title: Act 5, Scene 2 — Leonato’s Garden
paragraphs: [Enter Benedick and Margaret, meeting.]
BENEDICK. I pray you, sweet Mistress Margaret, deserve well at my hands by helping me to speech with Beatrice.
MARGARET. Will you then write me a sonnet in praise of my beauty?
BENEDICK. In so high a style, Margaret, that no man living shall come over it; for, in most comely truth, you deserve it.
MARGARET. To have no man come over me! Why, shall I always keep below stairs?
BENEDICK. Your wit is as quick as the greyhound's mouth; it catches.
MARGARET. And yours as blunt as the fencer's foils, which hit, but hurt not.
BENEDICK. A most manly wit, Margaret; it will not hurt a woman. And so, I pray you, call Beatrice. I give you the bucklers.
MARGARET. Give us the swords, we have bucklers of our own.
BENEDICK. If you use them, Margaret, you must put in the pikes with a vice; and they are dangerous weapons for maids.
MARGARET. Well, I will call Beatrice to you, who I think has legs.
BENEDICK. And therefore will come.
[Exit Margaret.]
The god of love, that sits above, and knows me, and knows me, how pitiful I deserve—

I mean, in singing: but in loving, Leander the good swimmer, Troilus the first employer of go-betweens, and a whole book full of these onetime carpet-mongers, whose names yet run smoothly in the even road of a blank verse—why, they were never so truly turned over and over as my poor self in love. By the Mass, I cannot show it in rhyme; I have tried. I can find no rhyme to 'lady' but 'baby,' an innocent rhyme; for 'scorn,' 'horn,' a hard rhyme; for 'school,' 'fool,' a babbling rhyme; very ominous endings. No, I was not born under a rhyming planet, nor can I woo in festival terms.
[Enter Beatrice.]
Sweet Beatrice, would you come when I called you?
BEATRICE. Yes, signior; and depart when you bid me.
BENEDICK. O, stay only till then!
BEATRICE. 'Then' is spoken; fare you well now. And yet, before I go, let me go with that I came for; which is, with knowing what has passed between you and Claudio.
BENEDICK. Only foul words; and thereupon I will kiss you.
BEATRICE. Foul words is but foul wind, and foul wind is but foul breath, and foul breath is noisome; therefore I will depart unkissed.

BENEDICK. You have frightened the word out of its right sense, so forceful is your wit. But I must tell you plainly, Claudio is undergoing my challenge, and either I must shortly hear from him, or I will subscribe him a coward. And, I pray you now, tell me, for which of my bad parts did you first fall in love with me?

BEATRICE. For them all together; which maintained so politic a state of evil that they will not admit any good part to intermingle with them. But for which of my good parts did you first suffer love for me?
BENEDICK. 'Suffer love'—a good epithet! I do suffer love indeed, for I love you against my will.
BEATRICE. In spite of your heart, I think. Alas, poor heart! If you spite it for my sake, I will spite it for yours; for I will never love that which my friend hates.
BENEDICK. You and I are too wise to woo peaceably.
BEATRICE. It appears not in this confession: there's not one wise man among twenty that will praise himself.

BENEDICK. An old, an old instance, Beatrice, that lived in the time of good neighbors. If a man does not erect in this age his own tomb before he dies, he shall live no longer in monument than the bell rings and the widow weeps.
BEATRICE. And how long is that, do you think?

BENEDICK. Question: why, an hour in clamor and a quarter in tears. Therefore it is most expedient for the wise—if Don Worm, his conscience, finds no impediment to the contrary—to be the trumpet of his own virtues, as I am to myself. So much for praising myself, who, I myself will bear witness, is praiseworthy. And now tell me, how does your cousin?
BEATRICE. Very ill.
BENEDICK. And how do you?
BEATRICE. Very ill too.
BENEDICK. Serve God, love me, and mend. There I will leave you too, for here comes one in haste.
[Enter Ursula.]

URSULA. Madam, you must come to your uncle. Yonder's old uproar at home. It is proved, my Lady Hero has been falsely accused, the Prince and Claudio mightily abused; and Don John is the author of all, who has fled and gone. Will you come presently?
BEATRICE. Will you go hear this news, signior?
BENEDICK. I will live in your heart, die in your lap, and be buried in your eyes; and moreover I will go with you to your uncle's.
[Exit.]

chapters.title: Act 5, Scene 3 — The Inside of a Church
paragraphs: [Enter Don Pedro, Claudio, and Attendants, with music and tapers.]
CLAUDIO. Is this the monument of Leonato?
A LORD. It is, my lord.
CLAUDIO.
[Reads from a scroll.]
Epitaph.
Done to death by slanderous tongues was the Hero that here lies. Death, in reward of her wrongs, gives her fame which never dies. So the life that died with shame lives in death with glorious fame.
Hang there upon the tomb,
Praising her when I am dumb. Now, music, sound, and sing your solemn hymn.
Song.

Pardon, goddess of the night, those that slew your virgin knight; for which, with songs of woe, round about her tomb they go. Midnight, assist our moan; help us to sigh and groan, heavily, heavily. Graves, yawn and yield your dead, till death be uttered, heavily, heavily.
CLAUDIO. Now, unto your bones good night! Yearly will I do this rite.

DON PEDRO. Good morrow, masters: put your torches out. The wolves have preyed; and look, the gentle day, before the wheels of Phoebus, round about dapples the drowsy East with spots of grey. Thanks to you all, and leave us: fare you well.
CLAUDIO. Good morrow, masters: each his several way.
DON PEDRO. Come, let us go hence, and put on other garments; and then to Leonato's we will go.
CLAUDIO. And may Hymen now with happier outcome speed us, than this for whom we rendered up this woe!
[Exit.]

chapters.title: Act 5, Scene 4 — A Room in Leonato’s House
paragraphs: [Enter Leonato, Antonio, Benedick, Beatrice, Margaret, Ursula, Friar Francis, and Hero.]
FRIAR. Did I not tell you she was innocent?

LEONATO. So are the Prince and Claudio, who accused her upon the error that you heard debated. But Margaret was in some fault for this, although against her will, as it appears in the true course of all the questioning.
ANTONIO. Well, I am glad that all things sort so well.
BENEDICK. And so am I, being else by faith forced to call young Claudio to a reckoning for it.
LEONATO. Well, daughter, and you gentlewomen all, withdraw into a chamber by yourselves, and when I send for you, come here masked. The Prince and Claudio promised by this hour to visit me.
[Exit Ladies.]
You know your office, brother. You must be father to your brother's daughter, and give her to young Claudio.
ANTONIO. Which I will do with steady countenance.
BENEDICK. Friar, I must ask your help, I think.
FRIAR. To do what, signior?
BENEDICK. To bind me, or undo me; one of them. Signior Leonato, the truth is, good signior, your niece regards me with an eye of favor.
LEONATO. That eye my daughter lent her. It is most true.
BENEDICK. And I do, with an eye of love, repay her.
LEONATO. The sight of which, I think, you had from me, from Claudio, and the Prince. But what is your will?

BENEDICK. Your answer, sir, is enigmatical. But, as for my will, my will is that your good will may stand with ours, this day to be joined in the state of honorable marriage. In which, good friar, I shall desire your help.
LEONATO. My heart is with your liking.
FRIAR. And my help. Here comes the Prince and Claudio.
[Enter Don Pedro and Claudio, with Attendants.]
DON PEDRO. Good morrow to this fair assembly.
LEONATO. Good morrow, Prince; good morrow, Claudio. We attend you here. Are you yet determined today to marry with my brother's daughter?
CLAUDIO. I'll hold my mind, even were she an Ethiope.
LEONATO. Call her forth, brother: here's the friar ready.
[Exit Antonio.]
DON PEDRO. Good morrow, Benedick. Why, what's the matter, that you have such a February face, so full of frost, of storm and cloudiness?

CLAUDIO. I think he thinks upon the savage bull. Tush! Fear not, man, we'll tip your horns with gold, and all Europa shall rejoice at you, as once Europa did at lusty Jove, when he would play the noble beast in love.
BENEDICK. Bull Jove, sir, had an amiable bellow; and some such strange bull leaped your father's cow, and got a calf in that same noble feat, much like to you, for you have just his bleat.
CLAUDIO. For this I owe you: here comes other reckonings.
[Re-enter Antonio, with the ladies masked.]
Which is the lady I must seize upon?
ANTONIO. This same is she, and I do give you her.
CLAUDIO. Why then, she's mine. Sweet, let me see your face.
LEONATO. No, that you shall not, till you take her hand before this friar, and swear to marry her.
CLAUDIO. Give me your hand: before this holy friar, I am your husband, if you like of me.
HERO. And when I lived, I was your other wife:
[Unmasking.] And when you loved, you were my other husband.
CLAUDIO. Another Hero!
HERO. Nothing more certain. One Hero died defiled, but I do live, and surely as I live, I am a maid.
DON PEDRO. The former Hero! Hero that is dead!
LEONATO. She died, my lord, but only while her slander lived.
FRIAR. All this amazement I can clarify. When the holy rites are ended, I'll tell you at length of fair Hero's death. Meantime, let wonder seem familiar, and to the chapel let us go presently.
BENEDICK. Soft and fair, friar. Which is Beatrice?
BEATRICE.
[Unmasking.] I answer to that name. What is your will?
BENEDICK. Do you not love me?
BEATRICE. Why, no; no more than reason.
BENEDICK. Why then, your uncle and the Prince and Claudio have been deceived; for they swore you did.
BEATRICE. Do you not love me?
BENEDICK. Truth, no; no more than reason.
BEATRICE. Why then, my cousin, Margaret, and Ursula are much deceived; for they did swear you did.
BENEDICK. They swore that you were almost sick for me.
BEATRICE. They swore that you were very near dead for me.
BENEDICK. It is no such matter. Then you do not love me?
BEATRICE. No, truly, except in friendly recompense.
LEONATO. Come, cousin, I am sure you love the gentleman.
CLAUDIO. And I'll be sworn upon it that he loves her; for here's a paper written in his hand, a halting sonnet of his own pure brain, fashioned to Beatrice.
HERO. And here's another, written in my cousin's hand, stolen from her pocket, containing her affection toward Benedick.
BENEDICK. A miracle! Here's our own hands against our hearts. Come, I will have you; but, by this light, I take you for pity.
BEATRICE. I would not deny you; but, by this good day, I yield upon great persuasion, and partly to save your life, for I was told you were in a consumption.
BENEDICK. Peace! I will stop your mouth. [Kisses her.]
DON PEDRO. How do you, Benedick, the married man?

BENEDICK. I'll tell you what, Prince: a college of wit-crackers cannot flout me out of my humor. Do you think I care for a satire or an epigram? No; if a man will be beaten with brains, he shall wear nothing handsome about him. In brief, since I do propose to marry, I will think nothing to any purpose that the world can say against it; and therefore never flout at me for what I have said against it, for man is a giddy thing, and this is my conclusion. For your part, Claudio, I did think to have beaten you; but, since you are like to be my kinsman, live unbruised, and love my cousin.

CLAUDIO. I had well hoped you would have denied Beatrice, that I might have cudgeled you out of your single life, to make you a double-dealer; which, without question, you will be, if my cousin does not look exceedingly closely to you.
BENEDICK. Come, come, we are friends. Let's have a dance before we are married, that we may lighten our own hearts and our wives' heels.
LEONATO. We'll have dancing afterward.
BENEDICK. First, on my word; therefore play, music! Prince, you are sad; get yourself a wife, get yourself a wife. There is no staff more reverent than one tipped with horn.
[Enter Messenger.]
MESSENGER. My lord, your brother John is taken in flight, and brought with armed men back to Messina.
BENEDICK. Don't think on him till tomorrow. I'll devise you brave punishments for him. Strike up, pipers!
[Dance. Exit.]
